metadata.title: ENISA - Technical Implementation Guidance for the NIS2 Directive
metadata.remarks: Guidance on the implementation of the technical and methodological requirements of the cybersecurity risk-management measures according to the NIS2 Directive and the Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690.

groups.title: 1. POLICY ON THE SECURITY OF NETWORK AND INFORMATION SYSTEMS
1.1 POLICY ON THE SECURITY OF NETWORK AND INFORMATION SYSTEMS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of Article 21(2), point (a) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the policy on the security of network and information systems shall:[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: set out the relevant entities’ approach to managing the security of their network and information systems;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: be appropriate to and complementary with the relevant entities’ business strategy and objectives;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: set out network and information security objectives;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: include a commitment to continual improvement of the security of network and information systems;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: include a commitment to provide the appropriate resources needed for its implementation, including the necessary staff, financial resources, processes, tools and technologies;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: be communicated to and acknowledged by relevant employees and relevant interested external parties;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: lay down roles and responsibilities pursuant to point 1.2;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: list the documentation to be kept and the duration of retention of the documentation;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: list the topic-specific policies;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: lay down indicators and measures to monitor its implementation and the current status of relevant entities’ maturity level of network and information security;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: indicate the date of the formal approval by the management bodies of the relevant entities (the ‘management bodies’).[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Set a policy on the security of network and information systems, covering all systems, assets and procedures that fall within the scope of the policy.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that relevant personnel and relevant interested external parties, acknowledge the policy on the security of network and information systems, typically through a signed document or digital acknowledgement, where applicable.[cite: 5]
  * Depending on the context, external parties may mean suppliers, service providers, shareholders, authorities, visitors, external interest groups or forums.[cite: 5]
  * The acknowledgement may be included in other contracts, such as employment contracts or service provision contracts.[cite: 5]
  * The policy should be communicated to relevant personnel and interested external parties in a form that is relevant, accessible and understandable to the intended reader.[cite: 5]
  * Relevant personnel and relevant interested external parties may not be made aware of the full text of the policy. Depending on their role, an extract or a summary containing only relevant information should be communicated and acknowledged. If the policy is distributed outside the entity, care should be taken not to disclose confidential information.[cite: 5]
  * For contractual requirements of direct suppliers and service providers, point 5.1.4 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that personnel are aware of their responsibilities for the security of network and information systems.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that the policy on the security of network and information systems is approved by the management bodies.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that the topic-specific policies are approved by an appropriate level of management.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that the policy includes detailed guidance on the procedures for managing policy exceptions.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented policy on the security of network and information systems which contains the elements required by points 1.1.1 (a) to 1.1.1 (k) of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5]
* The date of the formal approval by the management bodies of the relevant entities, indicated in the policy on the security of network and information systems.[cite: 5]
* Where applicable, acknowledgement forms or employment contracts, signed by personnel, which confirm they have read and understood the security policies.[cite: 5]
* Where applicable, acknowledgement forms, service provision contracts or other contracts, signed by relevant interested external parties, which confirm they have read and understood the security policies.[cite: 5]
* Evidence that the management bodies understand their role, responsibilities and authorities regarding network and information security. This can include but is not limited to:[cite: 5]
  * allocation of resources for policy implementation;[cite: 5]
  * requests (e.g. announcements, emails and documents) to personnel to apply network and information security in accordance with the established policies and procedures; and[cite: 5]
  * any initiatives that indicate that management bodies promote improvement in the area of network and information security.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The network and information system security policy shall be reviewed and, where appropriate, updated by management bodies at least annually and when significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks occur. The result of the reviews shall be documented.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review the policy on the security of network and information systems at least annually, taking into account (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * updates to the risk assessment results and the risk treatment plan (Annex to the regulation, point 2.1.4);[cite: 5]
  * relevant changes in legislation (laws, regulations and other measures imposed by national competent authorities);[cite: 5]
  * recommendations provided by relevant authorities;[cite: 5]
  * relevant changes in industry good practices;[cite: 5]
  * feedback from interested parties;[cite: 5]
  * findings of compliance monitoring (section 2.2) and of independent reviews (Annex to the regulation, point 2.3), including policy violations or policy exceptions;[cite: 5]
  * incidents, even those affecting similar entities in the sector.[cite: 5]
* Update the policy on the security of network and information systems and topic-specific policies, in line with new findings that could affect the entity’s approach to managing information security, including (9):[cite: 5]
  * updates to the risk assessment results and the risk treatment plan (Annex to the regulation, point 2.1.4);[cite: 5]
  * changes to the network and information systems;[cite: 5]
  * changes to the environment of operation;[cite: 5]
  * problems identified during the implementation of the policy;[cite: 5]
  * findings of compliance monitoring (Annex to the regulation, point 2.2.1) and of independent reviews (Annex to the regulation, point 2.3), including policy violations or policy exceptions;[cite: 5]
  * the status of preventive and corrective actions;[cite: 5]
  * trends related to threats and vulnerabilities; and[cite: 5]
  * known reported security incidents.[cite: 5]
* All updates to the policy should be based on the covered entity's unique security risks identified through its risk assessment.[cite: 5]
* Obtain approval for the revised policy and the policy exceptions by the management bodies.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Review comments or change logs for the policy on the security of network and information systems and topic-specific policies.[cite: 5]
* Documentation of the review process of the requirements listed in point 1.1.1 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5]
* Up-to-date policy on the security of network and information systems and topic-specific policies.[cite: 5]
* Evidence that any updates to the policy on the security of network and information systems and any policy exceptions, are approved by management bodies and a record is kept.[cite: 5]
* Evidence that any updates to the topic-specific policies are approved by an appropriate level of management and a record is kept.[cite: 5]
* Records of the management review.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE TIPS

* Analyse the policy on the security of network and information systems for compliance with:[cite: 5]
  * legislative, regulatory and contractual requirements;[cite: 5]
  * awareness and training requirements (Annex to the regulation, points 8.1 and 8.2); and[cite: 5]
  * business continuity requirements (Annex to the regulation, point 4.1).[cite: 5]
* Define procedures to facilitate the implementation of the policy on the security of network and information systems and associated measures.[cite: 5]
* Examine documentation of post-incident reviews for significant incidents (10) that include participation and input from management bodies.[cite: 5]
* Ensure that the policy is:[cite: 5]
  * protected in terms of confidentiality (on a need-to-know basis), integrity, availability and authenticity;[cite: 5]
  * managed properly so the information is complete, correct, understandable, easily identifiable and retrievable.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE (TIPS)

* Documented policy on the security of network and information systems, including networks and services in scope, assets supporting them and the security objectives, including applicable laws and regulations, accessible to personnel.[cite: 5]
* Documented topic-specific policies, including applicable laws and regulations, accessible to relevant personnel.[cite: 5]
* Evidence of cybersecurity training of management, for instance:[cite: 5]
  * training records;[cite: 5]
  * workshop and seminar attendance; and[cite: 5]
  * continuous learning materials.[cite: 5]
* Internal communication logs, ad hoc reports or communication policy or records showing regular briefings or updates provided to management bodies regarding cybersecurity matters or during significant incidents.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As part of their policy on the security of network and information systems referred to in point 1.1, the relevant entities shall lay down responsibilities and authorities for network and information system security and assign them to roles, allocate them according to the relevant entities’ needs and communicate them to the management bodies.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Write job descriptions in a way that clearly outlines rights and responsibilities.[cite: 5]
* Assign security roles and responsibilities to personnel and include these roles in the organisational chart.[cite: 5]
* Describe roles and assign corresponding responsibilities (e.g. chief information security officer), based on the guidance of international frameworks and standards, including the European cybersecurity skills framework (ECSF) (11).[cite: 5]
* Ensure that the roles allocated are suitable for the size and business needs of the entity.[cite: 5]
* Formally appoint competent personnel in security roles. Ensure that these assigned persons are competent on the basis of appropriate education, training or experience.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Job descriptions.[cite: 5]
* List of security roles, who occupies them and contact information.[cite: 5]
* Formal appointment of the key security roles and responsibilities, for example, listed in the company organigram or management decision, etc.[cite: 5]
* List of appointments and description of responsibilities and tasks for security roles.[cite: 5]
* Evidence of competence of the assigned persons.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall require all personnel and third parties to apply network and information system security in accordance with the established network and information security policy, topic-specific policies and procedures of the relevant entities.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Make personnel aware of the security roles in the entity and when each role should be contacted.[cite: 5]
* Make personnel aware of their network and information system security obligations, according to their role. For the disciplinary process, see point 10.4 in the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5]
* Make relevant interested external parties aware of their network and information system security obligations.[cite: 5]
  * For contractual requirements of direct suppliers and service providers, see point 5.1.4 in the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5]
  * Consider third parties, which means external entities or organisations not directly involved in the operations of the entity in scope but that may still affect its network and information security. For examples of relevant interested external parties, consider the guidance in section 1.1.[cite: 5]
* The requirement that all personnel and third parties apply network and information system security should be communicated in a form that is relevant, accessible and understandable to the intended reader.[cite: 5]
  * The network and information security policy, topic-specific policies and procedures of the relevant entities do not necessarily need to be communicated in their entirety.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Awareness/dissemination material for personnel, explaining security roles and when/how they should be contacted.[cite: 5]
* Service level agreements (SLAs), contracting contracts, data-processing agreements or other types of contracts or agreements with third parties.[cite: 5]
* Acknowledgement from third parties in various forms (letters, emails, portals or other online options) confirming that they have received and understand their obligations related to network and information system security, where such requirements are not covered by contractual arrangements.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: At least one person shall report directly to the management bodies on matters of network and information system security.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Appoint a person (e.g. chief information security officer or information security manager) responsible for overseeing network and information security matters.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that this role is recognized and duly authorized by management bodies.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Up-to-date documentation of the structure of security role assignments and responsibilities.[cite: 5]
* Minutes from meetings with the management.[cite: 5]
* Evidence of business decisions made (e.g. investments in cybersecurity).[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Depending on the size of the relevant entities, network and information system security shall be covered by dedicated roles or duties carried out in addition to existing roles.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* It is often practical to have dedicated information security roles (e.g. a chief information security officer or security analysts) who focus solely on protecting the entity’s data and systems.[cite: 5]
* In entities with limited resources, information security responsibilities may be distributed among existing roles. For instance, information technology (IT) staff might take on security duties alongside their regular tasks. However, the persons assigned should have relevant experience and training to perform the roles and to exercise their responsibilities.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Verify the presence of dedicated security roles in larger entities.[cite: 5]
* Check if security responsibilities are assigned to existing roles in smaller entities.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Conflicting duties and conflicting areas of responsibility shall be segregated, where applicable.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Consider segregating conflicting duties and areas of responsibility to reduce opportunities for unauthorized or unintentional modification or misuse of the entity’s asset. As a minimum, consider that the reviewer (auditor) must be different from the personnel or the line of authority of the area under review.[cite: 5]
* The results of the risk assessment or the business impact analysis (BIA) could be used to identify potential conflicting duties and areas of responsibility.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Up-to-date documentation of the structure of security role assignments and responsibilities.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Roles, responsibilities and authorities shall be reviewed and, where appropriate, updated by management bodies at planned intervals and when significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks occur.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Regularly review and revise the structure of security roles and responsibilities, based on (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * significant incidents, if any;[cite: 5]
  * changes to the environment of operation, including changes to the network and information systems;[cite: 5]
  * organisational changes.[cite: 5]
* Where appropriate, updates should be approved by management bodies.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Up-to-date documentation of the structure of security role assignments and responsibilities, including version history.[cite: 5]
* Documentation of the review process, taking into account changes and past incidents.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE TIPS

* Make sure that the roles responsible for security roles are contactable in case of incidents.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that each role has its deputy or that measures ensuring continuity in the event of the role representative’s absence are in place, where possible.[cite: 5]
* Establish a clear reporting line from the designated security officer to senior management.[cite: 5]
* Ensure that security reporting is integrated into the entity’s overall risk management framework.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE (TIPS)

* Documented incident response procedures (Annex to the regulation, point 3.5.1) including clear procedures for contacting security roles during an incident.[cite: 5]
* Logs and records of past incidents to check if the security roles were contacted promptly and effectively.[cite: 5]
* Crisis management process and incident response records to check the involvement of the management.[cite: 5]
* Up-to-date organisational chart to check if it clearly shows the reporting structure, including the designated security officer and their direct line to senior management. The organisational chart should be dated and the person making the update should be noted.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of Article 21(2), point (a) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the relevant entities shall establish and maintain an appropriate risk management framework to identify and address the risks posed to the security of network and information systems.[cite: 5] The relevant entities shall perform and document risk assessments and, based on the results, establish, implement and monitor a risk treatment plan.[cite: 5] Risk assessment results and residual risks (12) shall be accepted by management bodies or, where applicable, by persons who are accountable and have the authority to manage risks, provided that the relevant entities ensure adequate reporting to the management bodies.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* The entity can use its current risk management framework or adopt a new one (13).[cite: 5] A risk management framework is the structured approach used by an entity to identify, assess, manage and mitigate its cybersecurity risks.[cite: 5]
* Create a risk treatment plan that associates the identified risks with assets and the measures mitigating the associated risks and takes into account, at least, elements (g) to (h) in point 2.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5] The plan should at least include:[cite: 5]
  * a description of the identified risk and how it can negatively affect security objectives;[cite: 5]
  * a risk treatment option (for example risk avoidance, risk mitigation, risk transfer or sharing or risk acceptance);[cite: 5]
  * the assets associated with the risk;[cite: 5]
  * the measures which mitigate the risk;[cite: 5]
  * a procedure for assessing the effectiveness of implementation of the measure(s);[cite: 5]
  * implementation timelines; and[cite: 5]
  * responsible roles.[cite: 5]
* Consider residual risks from third parties, for example, data breaches, unaddressed vulnerabilities, regulatory non-compliance from the from the third-party side and over-reliance on a single third party.[cite: 5]
* Ensure residual risks are accepted by management bodies or, where applicable, persons who are accountable and have the authority to manage risks, in line with the acceptable residual risk levels of the entity.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that management bodies or, where applicable, persons who are accountable and have the authority to manage risks approve the risk-assessment results and risk-treatment plan.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented risk management framework.[cite: 5]
* Documented results from previous risk assessments.[cite: 5]
* Documented risk treatment plan.[cite: 5]
* Record of approval of risk assessment results by management bodies or by persons who are accountable and have the authority to manage risks.[cite: 5]
* Record of approval of residual risks by management bodies or, where applicable, by persons who are accountable and have the authority to manage risks.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of point 2.1.1, the relevant entities shall establish procedures for identification, analysis, assessment and treatment of risks (‘cybersecurity risk management process’).[cite: 5] The cybersecurity risk management process shall be an integral part of the relevant entities’ overall risk management process, where applicable.[cite: 5] As part of the cybersecurity risk management process, the relevant entities shall:[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: follow a risk management methodology;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: establish the risk tolerance level in accordance with the risk appetite of the relevant entities;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: establish and maintain relevant risk criteria;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: in line with an all-hazards approach, identify and document the risks posed to the security of network and information systems, in particular in relation to third parties and risks that could lead to disruptions in the availability, integrity, authenticity and confidentiality of the network and information systems, including the identification of single point of failures;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: analyse the risks posed to the security of network and information systems, including threat, likelihood, impact and risk level, taking into account cyber threat intelligence and vulnerabilities;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: evaluate the identified risks based on the risk criteria;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: identify and prioritise appropriate risk treatment options and measures;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: continuously monitor the implementation of the risk treatment measures;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: identify who is responsible for implementing the risk treatment measures and when they should be implemented;[cite: 5]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: document the chosen risk treatment measures in a risk treatment plan and the reasons justifying the acceptance of residual risks in a comprehensible manner.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Select a risk management methodology (14).[cite: 5]
* Establish the entity’s risk appetite, that is the amount of risk that the entity is strategically willing to accept to achieve its objectives.[cite: 5] Criteria may include (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * business strategic objectives;[cite: 5]
  * stakeholder expectations;[cite: 5]
  * regulatory requirements; and[cite: 5]
  * organizational culture.[cite: 5]
* Define the risk tolerance level, which refers to the level of risk that an entity is willing to accept in pursuit of its long-term objectives.[cite: 5] Examples may include (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * acceptable downtime for systems for which criticality is high (e.g. up to two hours of downtime per month);[cite: 5]
  * tolerance for data loss (e.g. loss of data with low criticality within a 24-hour window);[cite: 5]
  * maximum financial loss that can be absorbed without jeopardizing operations (e.g. up to EUR 100,000 in recovery costs);[cite: 5]
  * willingness to invest a certain percentage of revenue in measures (e.g. 5% of annual revenue);[cite: 5]
  * adherence to regulatory obligations with specific penalties or fines influencing risk acceptance;[cite: 5]
  * acceptable level of customer dissatisfaction or negative media exposure from a data breach (e.g. tolerating one major incident every few years);[cite: 5]
  * acceptance of certain vulnerabilities based on risk mitigation measures in place (e.g. outdated software provided that it is monitored and patched regularly);[cite: 5]
  * time frame for responding to and recovering from incidents (e.g. a maximum of 48 hours for containment); and[cite: 5]
  * acceptance of minor incidents as part of normal operations while prioritizing major threats.[cite: 5]
* Define risk acceptance criteria, which may include (indicative, non-exhaustive list) (15):[cite: 5]
  * accepting risks categorized as low severity, such as minor data leaks that don't expose sensitive information;[cite: 5]
  * accepting risks assessed as having a low likelihood of occurrence (e.g. certain rare types of cyberattacks);[cite: 5]
  * accepting risks if the cost of mitigation exceeds the potential impact (e.g. not upgrading legacy systems if the upgrade cost is significantly higher than potential losses);[cite: 5]
  * accepting specific compliance risks if there is a plan in place to address them within a defined timeframe (e.g. temporarily accepting minor non-compliance with a commitment to remediate within six months);[cite: 5]
  * allowing certain risks in low-criticality systems or departments that do not affect core business operations (e.g. accepting a risk in a test environment);[cite: 5]
  * accepting certain vulnerabilities for a defined period while planning for remediation (e.g. accepting the risk of outdated software for three months until a full upgrade can be completed);[cite: 5]
  * accepting risks where the expected incident impact falls below a predetermined financial threshold (e.g. losses under EUR 50,000 accepted without further action);[cite: 5]
  * accepting risks after informing stakeholders and receiving their agreement, particularly if they understand the trade-offs involved; and[cite: 5]
  * accepting residual risks where existing measures reduce the likelihood or impact to an acceptable level (e.g. using encryption for sensitive data but accepting risks of loss due to user error).[cite: 5]
* Define risk criteria, that is, how the entity evaluates the significance of the risks that it identifies and makes decisions concerning risks.[cite: 5] Risk criteria may include (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * alignment with risk appetite: accepting risks that align with the organization's overall risk appetite, such as delays in internal reporting processes that do not impact customer service or compliance;[cite: 5]
  * regulatory and legal exposure: prioritizing risks based on potential legal or regulatory consequences, such as treating violations of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) involving customer data as high-risk due to potential fines and reputational damage;[cite: 5]
  * reputational impact: escalating risks that could significantly harm the organization's public image, such as incidents likely to attract media attention;[cite: 5]
  * risk velocity: giving higher priority to risks with high velocity, such as zero-day exploits that can be weaponised before patches are available;[cite: 5]
  * recovery complexity: treating risks as critical if they involve complex or time-consuming recovery, such as cyber-attacks on legacy systems with limited vendor support;[cite: 5]
  * emerging technology risks: Considering risks involving emerging technologies as higher priority, such as AI systems producing unexplainable or non-compliant decisions due to lack of transparency;[cite: 5]
  * stakeholder sensitivity: re-evaluating risks that concern key stakeholders, such as risks flagged by the board, regulators or major customers, even if the assessed technical risk is low.[cite: 5]
* Criteria for performing cybersecurity risk assessments refer to consequences, likelihood or level of risk.[cite: 5] These may refer to (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * the importance of assets;[cite: 5]
  * the severity of threats;[cite: 5]
  * the vulnerability of network and information systems (16);[cite: 5]
  * impact analysis;[cite: 5]
  * existing measures; and[cite: 5]
  * stakeholders concerns or requirements.[cite: 5]
* Make a list of the main risks for the security of network and information systems, taking into account the main threats to the assets in scope.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that each risk is associated with at least one:[cite: 5]
  * of the risk treatment options or a combination of them, in line with the results of the risk assessment and in accordance with the entity’s policy on the security of network and information systems (recital 11 of the regulation); and[cite: 5]
  * specific risk treatment measure.[cite: 5]
* Develop risk-treatment plans to address the elements in points (i) and (j) in point 2.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5]
* Assign responsibilities to appropriate individuals or teams for executing these risk treatment plans.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented cybersecurity risk-management process that takes into account elements referred to in point 2.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5]
* Documented risk-management methodology and/or tools that take into account at least elements (a) to (f) in point 2.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5]
* List of the main risks described at a high level, including underlying threat(s) and unaddressed vulnerabilities and their potential impact on the security of networks and services.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that the entity follows an all-hazards approach (check that the risk-assessment approach addresses a wide range of potential threats and risks, not just the cyber ones, but natural or man-made, accidental or intentional threats and risks).[cite: 5]
* Evidence that residual risks resulting from dependencies on third parties are listed and mitigated.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When identifying and prioritising appropriate risk treatment options and measures, the relevant entities shall take into account the risk assessment results, the results of the procedure to assess the effectiveness of cybersecurity risk-management measures, the cost of implementation in relation to the expected benefit, the asset classification referred to in point 12.1 and the business impact analysis referred to in point 4.1.3.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Make sure that personnel take into account the elements referred to in point 2.1.3 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Guidance for personnel on assessing risks that takes into account the elements referred to in point 2.1.3 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where appropriate, update the risk assessment results and the risk treatment plan at planned intervals and at least annually and when significant changes to operations or risks or significant incidents occur.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review risk assessment results and risk treatment at least annually taking into account:[cite: 5]
  * results of audits and previous reviews,[cite: 5]
  * status of implementation of the measures described in the risk treatment plan (see the policy on the assessment of the effectiveness of measures in line with the Annex to Regulation, point 7.1.1);[cite: 5]
  * changes to the information systems;[cite: 5]
  * changes to the environment of operation;[cite: 5]
  * post-incident review findings (section 3.6); and[cite: 5]
  * trends and changes related to threats and vulnerabilities, as they may affect risks.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documentation of the review process.[cite: 5]
* Review comments or change logs for the risk assessment and risk treatment plan.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE TIPS

* Ensure that key personnel use the risk management methodology and tools.[cite: 5]
* Overall, the entity has four risk treatment options associated with each risk.[cite: 5] Each option should be accompanied by specific risk treatment measures (indicative, non-exhaustive list of examples):[cite: 5]
  * Risk avoidance: as a measure to treat this risk, the entity might choose to eliminate activities or conditions that expose the entity to this risk, for example, discontinuing the use of a vulnerable software application.[cite: 5]
  * Risk mitigation: as a measure to treat this risk, the entity might choose to implement measures to reduce the likelihood or impact of such a risk.[cite: 5] This can include installing firewalls, using encryption and conducting regular security training for employees.[cite: 5]
  * Risk transfer or sharing: as a measure to treat this risk, the entity might choose to shift parts of the risk impact to another party, typically through insurance or outsourcing certain functions to third-party providers.[cite: 5] However, it is important to note that such arrangements do not eliminate the entity’s overall accountability or legal obligations regarding the risk.[cite: 5] For instance, purchasing cyber insurance may cover potential data breach costs, but the entity remains responsible for implementing appropriate security measures and complying with data protection regulations.[cite: 5]
  * Risk acceptance: as a measure to treat this risk, the entity might choose to acknowledge the risk and decide to accept it without taking any specific action, often because the cost of mitigation is higher than the potential impact.[cite: 5] This approach is usually accompanied by a contingency plan to manage the risk if it materialises.[cite: 5] The approach should be clearly documented, supported by a realistic estimation of potential costs and including financial provisions to address the impact should the risk materialise.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that the risk from vulnerabilities assigned to the highest classification (e.g. ‘critical’ in the common vulnerability scoring system (CVSS)) or equivalent is not accepted, if possible (section 6.10).[cite: 5]
* Concerning the risk treatment plans, the entity might additionally take into account:[cite: 5]
  * findings of the review;[cite: 5]
  * implementation steps; and[cite: 5]
  * resources needed.[cite: 5]
* Manage any exceptions in the risk treatment plans’ implementation.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE (TIPS)

* Documented action plans developed in response to review findings.[cite: 5]
* Key personnel knowing the main risks (e.g. evidence from emails, interviews and awareness-raising sessions).[cite: 5]
* Documented risk treatment plan implementation exceptions.[cite: 5]
* Risk register.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall regularly review the compliance with their policies on network and information system security, topic-specific policies, rules and standards.[cite: 5] The management bodies shall be informed of the status of network and information security on the basis of the compliance reviews by means of regular reporting.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Develop a standardized report format for reporting to management bodies.[cite: 5] Consider the following elements (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * key metrics,[cite: 5]
  * compliance status, including policy exceptions,[cite: 5]
  * identified risks and[cite: 5]
  * recommended actions.[cite: 5]
* Reports are generated and presented to management bodies at least annually.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Recent compliance review reports.[cite: 5]
* Logs of policy exceptions.[cite: 5] Examples of such exceptions include, among others, the situations mentioned in the second paragraph of Article 2(2) and those under recital 5 of the regulation.[cite: 5] Other examples include (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * software updates: if a system relies on an older version of software that is incompatible with the latest update, an exception might be granted to delay the update until a compatible solution is found;[cite: 5]
  * access control: if a particular user or system cannot support an authentication mechanism (e.g. multi-factor authentication (MFA)) due to technical limitations, an exception might be granted while alternative measures are implemented; and[cite: 5]
  * encryption: if a legacy system does not support encryption, an exception might be granted until the system is replaced.[cite: 5]
* Records of the exception request and approval, along with details of the compensatory controls implemented.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall put in place an effective compliance reporting system which shall be appropriate to their structures, operating environments and threat landscapes.[cite: 5] The compliance reporting system shall be capable to provide to the management bodies an informed view of the current state of the relevant entities’ management of risks.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Set up procedures for compliance monitoring, including (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * objectives and a high-level approach to compliance monitoring;[cite: 5]
  * relevant security policies that are subject to compliance monitoring;[cite: 5]
  * the frequency of compliance reviews;[cite: 5]
  * who should carry out compliance reviews (internal or external); and[cite: 5]
  * templates for compliance review reports.[cite: 5]
* Analyse and evaluate the results of the compliance review.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented procedures for monitoring compliance.[cite: 5]
* Documented analysis and evaluation of the results, including the current state of the entity’s risk management.[cite: 5]
* Detailed compliance monitoring plans, including long-term, high-level objectives and planning.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall perform the compliance monitoring at planned intervals and when significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks occur.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Compliance monitoring should take place at least annually, taking into account:[cite: 5]
  * significant incidents, if any;[cite: 5]
  * changes to the environment of operation;[cite: 5]
  * changes to the threat landscape and cybersecurity legal and regulatory requirements;[cite: 5]
  * changes to standards; and[cite: 5]
  * changes to the policy on the security of network and information systems and/or topic-specific policies.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Any corrective actions resulting from the assessments and tests, including changes to the measures made by the entity once the effectiveness of the measures has been assessed in line with the Annex to the regulation, point 7.1.1.[cite: 5]
* Evidence that reports of lessons learned or root cause analysis of past incidents, if any, were taken into account.[cite: 5]

groups.title: 2.3 INDEPENDENT REVIEW OF INFORMATION AND NETWORK SECURITY

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review independently their approach to managing network and information system security and its implementation including people, processes and technologies.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Make sure that the independent review is conducted by a person or persons with the appropriate competences (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * cybersecurity technical knowledge, for example cybersecurity frameworks (ISO/IEC 27001, National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) cybersecurity framework, etc.),[cite: 5]
  * industry knowledge,[cite: 5]
  * risk assessment skills,[cite: 5]
  * compliance and regulatory knowledge, for example the NIS2 Directive, the GDPR and the Digital Operational Resilience Act,[cite: 5]
  * good understanding of good practices in auditing and[cite: 5]
  * good understanding of when technical certification and conformance are required and must be documented in the conformance and compliance report, to ensure that global standards are implemented correctly.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented results of the review or audit.[cite: 5]
* Evidence of the competences of the independent reviewers, for example professional experience and academic qualifications, certifications such as certified information systems auditor, certified information systems security professional, certified information security manager, etc.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall develop and maintain processes to conduct independent reviews which shall be carried out by individuals with appropriate audit competence.[cite: 5] Where the independent review is conducted by staff members of the relevant entity, the persons conducting the reviews shall not be in the line of authority of the personnel of the area under review.[cite: 5] If the size of the relevant entities does not allow such separation of line of authority, the relevant entities shall put in place alternative measures to guarantee the impartiality of the reviews.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Set up a process for independent review of information and network security, including (indicative and non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * scope and purpose of the independent reviews (e.g. compliance, risk assessment, policy adherence);[cite: 5]
  * methodology of the reviews (e.g. standardised checklist, standard based, ad hoc, how it addresses processes that will be tested in real time for conformance (e.g. cloud service) or those that will be periodically evaluated);[cite: 5]
  * review committee’s role;[cite: 5]
  * frequency of the independent reviews;[cite: 5]
  * who should carry out independent reviews (internal or external); and[cite: 5]
  * templates for independent review reports.[cite: 5]
* Maintain independence in line with point 2.3.2 of the Annex to the regulation;[cite: 5]
* Where appropriate, consider alternative measures to the separation of line of authority (indicative and non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * review personnel rotation;[cite: 5]
  * set up a review committee with members from different departments;[cite: 5]
  * external third-party review service provider.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented process for independent review of information and network security.[cite: 5]
* Conflict of interest declarations.[cite: 5]
* Contracts with external third-party review service providers.[cite: 5]
* Detailed independent review plans.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The results of the independent reviews, including the results from the compliance monitoring pursuant to point 2.2. and the monitoring and measurement pursuant to point 7, shall be reported to the management bodies.[cite: 5] Corrective actions shall be taken or residual risk accepted according to the relevant entities’ risk acceptance criteria.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Analyse and evaluate the results of the independent review.[cite: 5]
* Report results to management bodies.[cite: 5]
* Use a standardized report format for reporting to the management bodies.[cite: 5] Consider the following elements (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 5]
  * executive summary, including the scope and key findings,[cite: 5]
  * methodology,[cite: 5]
  * detailed findings, including gaps identified and non-compliance issues,[cite: 5]
  * conclusions,[cite: 5]
  * recommendations and[cite: 5]
* Reports are generated and presented to management bodies at least annually.[cite: 5]
* Take corrective actions or justify, accept and document residual risks.[cite: 5]
* The outcomes of independent reviews should be systematically reflected in the risk assessment results and risk treatment plans (Annex to the regulation, point 2.1).[cite: 5] Specifically, when a risk is identified or reassessed through an independent review, the corresponding risk assessment should be updated accordingly.[cite: 5] This ensures that the risk profile remains accurate and that any emerging or evolving risks are adequately captured and addressed in the overall risk management framework.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented analysis and evaluation of the results, including any residual risks.[cite: 5]
* Minutes from past reviews.[cite: 5]
* Any corrective actions resulting from the assessments and tests, including changes to the measures made by the entity once the effectiveness of the measures has been assessed in line with the Annex to the regulation, point 7.1.1.[cite: 5]
* Documentation of any corrective actions.[cite: 5]
* Budget approval for any corrective actions.[cite: 5]
* The most recent results of compliance monitoring and auditing.[cite: 5]
* Records from updated risk register.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The independent reviews shall take place at planned intervals and when significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks occur.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Independent reviews should take place at least annually, taking into account:[cite: 5]
  * significant incidents, if any;[cite: 5]
  * changes to the environment of operation;[cite: 5]
  * changes to the threat landscape and cybersecurity legal and regulatory requirements; and[cite: 5]
  * changes to the policy on the security of network and information systems and/or topic-specific policies.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Independent review reports documenting findings, recommendations and actions taken in response.[cite: 5]
* Summaries of previous independent reviews, highlighting the scope and frequency.[cite: 5]
* Records of significant incidents that occurred in the past year, along with any corresponding review or analysis documentation.[cite: 5]
* Annual independent review plans or schedules that outline the scope of independent reviews and the specific measures being evaluated.[cite: 5]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE TIPS

* Make sure that the independent review process is approved by management bodies.[cite: 5]
* Make sure that the results of the review are approved by management bodies.[cite: 5]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE (TIPS)

* Documented procedures approved by management bodies.[cite: 5]
* Approval of the residual risks by management bodies.[cite: 5]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of Article 21(2), point (b) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the relevant entities shall establish and implement an incident handling policy laying down the roles, responsibilities and procedures for detecting, analysing, containing or responding to, recovering from, documenting and reporting of incidents in a timely manner.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Define clear objectives for the incident handling policy.[cite: 4]
* Ensure the policy complies with relevant laws, regulations and industry standards (17).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented incident handling policy that contains, at least, the elements referred to in point 3.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Documented standards and/or good practices that are taken into consideration for this policy.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy referred to in point 3.1.1 shall be coherent with the business continuity and disaster recovery plan referred to in point 4.1.[cite: 4] The policy shall include:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: a categorisation system for incidents that is consistent with the event assessment and classification carried out pursuant to point 3.4.1;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: effective communication plans including for escalation and reporting;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: assignment of roles to detect and appropriately respond to incidents to competent employees;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: documents to be used in the course of incident detection and response such as incident response manuals, escalation charts, contact lists and templates.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Align the incident handling policy with the business continuity and disaster recovery plan (Annex to the regulation, point 4.1) by (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * ensuring that they aim to minimise disruptions, protect assets and ensure a swift return to normal operations;[cite: 4]
  * identifying interfaces between the incident handling policy and business continuity management;[cite: 4]
  * describing workflows which trigger business continuity (Annex to the regulation, points 4.1, 4.2 or 4.3) during an incident; and[cite: 4]
  * developing scenarios that test the interaction between these processes and describe the result of this interaction in the incident handling policy.[cite: 4]
* Set up a categorisation system for incidents, which refers to the scheme that the entity uses to identify the consequences and the priority of an incident, together with the criteria for categorising events as incidents (18).[cite: 4] An indicative, non-exhaustive list of criteria might include one or more of the following:[cite: 4]
  * impact on business operations,[cite: 4]
  * data sensitivity in accordance with risk management,[cite: 4]
  * legal and regulatory impact, including reporting timelines stemming from regulatory framework e.g. GDPR, national regulations,[cite: 4]
  * scope and scale meaning the evaluation of how widespread the event is,[cite: 4]
  * type of attack (19),[cite: 4]
  * criticality of the systems affected,[cite: 4]
  * malicious software/vulnerability exploitation,[cite: 4]
  * impact on human lives and safety and[cite: 4]
  * incident containment urgency,[cite: 4]
  * likelihood of recovery,[cite: 4]
  * potential of data exfiltration or corruption, such as in the case of ransomware,[cite: 4]
  * other criteria on what constitutes a significant incident as per this regulation.[cite: 4]
* Ensure that the incident handling policy refers to different types of incidents such as (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * system failures and loss of service availability;[cite: 4]
  * malicious code;[cite: 4]
  * denial of service;[cite: 4]
  * errors;[cite: 4]
  * breaches of confidentiality and integrity; and[cite: 4]
  * misuse of network and information systems.[cite: 4]
* Communicate the incident to relevant stakeholders and personnel according to a communication plan.[cite: 4] The communication plan should consider the event reporting mechanism (Annex to the regulation, point 3.3) and may include (indicative, non-exhaustive list) the following:[cite: 4]
  * purpose and scope of the plan,[cite: 4]
  * roles and responsibilities for communication tasks,[cite: 4]
  * list of internal and external stakeholders to be informed,[cite: 4]
  * reporting timelines stemming from regulatory framework, e.g. GDPR, national regulations,[cite: 4]
  * conditions and procedures for escalation of incidents,[cite: 4]
  * channels to be used for communication (e.g. email, intranet, phone calls, social media, press releases),[cite: 4]
  * channels of communication need to be tailored based on the target audience (that is internal, client or general public, etc.),[cite: 4]
  * methods for stakeholders to provide feedback or ask questions and[cite: 4]
  * guidelines for when to communicate and the frequency of updates, along with pre-drafted message templates for various scenarios and the core messages to be communicated.[cite: 4]
* Identify the necessary roles and responsibilities to be assigned for incident handling.[cite: 4] The entities can use already established skills frameworks, for example the ECSF, to assist them in identifying the necessary skills and knowledge.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Cross references between the incident handling policy and the business continuity and disaster recovery plan, if available.[cite: 4]
* Records of testing and drills that involve both incident handling and business continuity / disaster recovery.[cite: 4]
* Interviews with key personnel involved in incident response, business continuity and disaster recovery.[cite: 4]
* An incident categorisation system.[cite: 4]
* Evidence that the incident handling policy is in place and communicated to employees.[cite: 4]
* Evidence that a communication plan for incident handling is in place.[cite: 4]
* Procedures for how to communicate the incident to relevant authorities and the computer security incident response team (CSIRT) are in place.[cite: 4]
* Procedures for how to communicate the incident to customers or how and when to involve a supplier (if applicable).[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The roles, responsibilities and procedures laid down in the policy shall be tested and reviewed and, where appropriate, updated at planned intervals and after significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Consider one or more of the following to test the entity’s incident handling policy (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * tabletop exercise,[cite: 4]
  * simulation of an incident, preferably based on a selected attack scenario based on identified risks and the current threat landscape,[cite: 4]
  * red team/blue team exercise and[cite: 4]
  * past incident walk-through.[cite: 4]
* Test the roles, responsibilities and procedures laid down in the policy at least annually.[cite: 4]
* Review and update roles, responsibilities and procedures laid down in the policy at least annually, taking into account the following, in addition to the elements referred to in point 3.1.3 of the Annex to the regulation:[cite: 4]
  * results from the policy tests,[cite: 4]
  * changes to the threat landscape and cybersecurity legal and regulatory requirements and[cite: 4]
  * changes to the policy on the security of network and information systems and/or topic-specific policies.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Periodic simulations and awareness raising activities to assess the readiness of personnel and the adequacy of the procedures.[cite: 4]
* Incident handling policy testing plans or schedules.[cite: 4]
* Incident handling policy review plans or schedules.[cite: 4]
* Procedure updates (version history), if available.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE TIPS

* Identify and consider all internal and external resources required in the event of an incident and ensure their availability at any time:[cite: 4]
  * make sure that personnel are properly trained to handle and manage incidents;[cite: 4]
  * identify and consider all external stakeholders (e.g. operators, technology suppliers, free and open source (20) project contacts, national competent authorities or CSIRTs) necessary for incident handling.[cite: 4]
* Changes in the policy should be communicated to the relevant personnel.[cite: 4]
* Ensure a clear overview of the various incident reporting obligations that the entity must fulfil under different reporting regimes.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE (TIPS)

* Detailed procedures for the incident handling policy communicated to personnel as appropriate.[cite: 4]
* A list of reporting obligations and deadlines, which may cover both legal and contractual obligations.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall lay down procedures and use tools to monitor and log activities on their network and information systems to detect events that could be considered as incidents and respond accordingly to mitigate the impact.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Identify one or more objectives of monitoring and logging (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * threat detection,[cite: 4]
  * compliance assurance,[cite: 4]
  * incident response support,[cite: 4]
  * performance optimisation,[cite: 4]
  * anomaly detection,[cite: 4]
  * monitor for new vulnerability reports issued for any free and open source software components (21) used by the entity,[cite: 4]
  * data loss prevention,[cite: 4]
  * forensic investigations support and[cite: 4]
  * network health monitoring.[cite: 4]
* Procedures should describe (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * objectives,[cite: 4]
  * data for collection and relevant tools,[cite: 4]
  * description of data algorithms and[cite: 4]
  * mechanisms for notifying the relevant personnel.[cite: 4]
* Select tools that serve the objectives of monitoring and logging according to specific criteria (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * ease of use,[cite: 4]
  * integration with the existing network and information system, including cross-border operations and the associated regulatory, security and performance considerations,[cite: 4]
  * minimisation of manual intervention,[cite: 4]
  * capability of collecting data from various sources, for example networks, systems and applications,[cite: 4]
  * security features offered, for example encryption and access control and[cite: 4]
  * costs and licencing.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Procedures in place.[cite: 4]
* Tools in place.[cite: 4]
* Configuration settings of the logging function that serve the identified objectives.[cite: 4]
* Configuration settings of the logging function in line with documented standards and/or good practices.[cite: 4]
* Safeguards to protect the confidentiality, integrity and availability of logs.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To the extent feasible, monitoring shall be automated and carried out either continuously or in periodic intervals, subject to business capabilities.[cite: 4] The relevant entities shall implement their monitoring activities in a way which minimises false positives and false negatives.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* To minimise false positives and false negatives, to the extent feasible, consider one or more of the following (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * establish network traffic patterns;[cite: 4]
  * use analytics and machine learning algorithms;[cite: 4]
  * continuously update the automated monitoring tools to adapt to new threats and changes in the environment; and[cite: 4]
  * fine-tune the parameters and thresholds based on the latest data and feedback.[cite: 4]
* Where appropriate, ensure that all potential risks are properly covered by relevant use cases, for example use case for access to critical data, use case for data exfiltration or use case for ransomware infection, so that no critical threat goes undetected.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Acceptable log monitoring, collection, storage and analysis tools, in line with the state of the art.[cite: 4]
* Security Incident and Event Management (SIEM) systems used to analyse data and identify deviations from established patterns.[cite: 4]
* Endpoint detection and response (EDR) and Extended Detection and Response (XDR) tools in place.[cite: 4]
* Mechanisms that aim to minimise false positives and false negatives are in place.[cite: 4]
* Where appropriate, mapping use cases to potential risks to ensure comprehensive and effective monitoring.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the procedures referred to in point 3.2.1., the relevant entities shall maintain, document and review logs.[cite: 4] The relevant entities shall establish a list of assets to be subject to logging based on the results of the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1.[cite: 4] Where appropriate, logs shall include:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: relevant outbound and inbound network traffic;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: creation, modification or deletion of users of the relevant entities’ network and information systems and extension of the permissions;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: access to systems and applications;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: authentication-related events;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: all privileged access to systems and applications and activities performed by administrative accounts;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: access or changes to critical configuration and backup files;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: event logs and logs from security tools, such as antivirus, intrusion detection systems or firewalls;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: use of system resources, as well as their performance;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: physical access to facilities;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: access to and use of their network equipment and devices;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: activation, stopping and pausing of the various logs;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: environmental events.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* With regard to critical configuration, consider the settings and parameters that are vital for the proper functioning, security and performance of the entity’s network and information system.[cite: 4] These configurations are vital because any changes or misconfigurations might have a significant impact, including system outages, security vulnerabilities or reduced performance of the entity’s network and information system.[cite: 4]
* Consult the risk assessment results to determine which network traffic needs to be logged.[cite: 4] For example, if certain assets are identified as high risk (e.g. due to being potentially vulnerable or crucial to the business operation) their inbound and outbound traffic should be logged for monitoring and analysis.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Samples of log files containing the elements referred to in point 3.2.3 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Samples of log files containing current and historical domain name system (DNS) and dynamic host configuration protocol (DHCP) logs.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The logs shall be regularly reviewed for any unusual or unwanted trends.[cite: 4] Where appropriate, the relevant entities shall lay down appropriate values for alarm thresholds.[cite: 4] If the laid down values for alarm threshold are exceeded, an alarm shall be triggered, where appropriate, automatically.[cite: 4] The relevant entities shall ensure that, in case of an alarm, a qualified and appropriate response is initiated in a timely manner.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Consider the use of anomaly detection or adaptive alarm thresholds to complement traditional static rules.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that procedures are designed to detect network-based attacks based on anomalous inbound and outbound ingress or egress traffic patterns and/or denial of service (DoS) attacks, in a timely manner.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that alarm thresholds, where appropriate, have been set in alignment with the results of the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1, covering at least the situations in point 3.2.3 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4] An indicative, non-exhaustive list of examples with thresholds (22) follows:[cite: 4]
  * relevant outbound and inbound network traffic: traffic volume spikes exceeding 50% of normal traffic in a 10-minute period on a specific port;[cite: 4]
  * access to systems and applications: three or more account lockouts within 15 minutes;[cite: 4]
  * privileged access: two or more instances of privilege escalation (e.g. normal user to admin) within 24 hours (23);[cite: 4]
  * antivirus: malware is detected on multiple endpoints within a short timeframe;[cite: 4]
  * use of system resources: installations of unauthorised software within a short timeframe.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Regular reports that summarize log data and highlight any anomalies detected.[cite: 4]
* Alarm thresholds set.[cite: 4]
* Records from past alarm triggers when thresholds were exceeded.[cite: 4]
* Existing workflows that trigger event reporting (section 3.3).[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall maintain and back up logs for a predefined period and shall protect them from unauthorised access or changes.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Make sure that the log retention period is defined in accordance with business needs, the risk assessment results and legal requirements/obligations.[cite: 4]
* The backup logs’ maintenance period shouldn’t be shorter than the logs’ review period, referred to in point 3.2.4 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* The retention period should be in line with what is referred to in point 4.2.2 (f) of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Delete data when the retention period ends.[cite: 4]
* Consider mechanisms to protect logs from unauthorised access or changes (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * encryption,[cite: 4]
  * access control,[cite: 4]
  * hashing (section 9.2) and[cite: 4]
  * logging of all access and changes to log files.[cite: 4]
* The access control should be in line with what is referred to in point 4.2.2 (d) of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* A retention period is set.[cite: 4]
* The retention period is in line with what is referred to in point 4.2.2 (f) of the Annex to the regulation and is shorter than the logs’ review period, referred to in point 3.2.4 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Log management is in place.[cite: 4]
* Logs do not contain data about which retention periods have expired.[cite: 4]
* Access control mechanisms are in place.[cite: 4]
* Access control is in line with what is referred to in point 4.2.2 (d) of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: To the extent feasible, the relevant entities shall ensure that all systems have synchronised time sources to be able to correlate logs between systems for event assessment.[cite: 4] The relevant entities shall establish and keep a list of all assets that are being logged and ensure that monitoring and logging systems are redundant.[cite: 4] The availability of the monitoring and logging systems shall be monitored independent of the systems they are monitoring.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Consider the following for time synchronisation:[cite: 4]
  * Utilize Network Time Protocol (NTP) servers or Precision Time Protocol (PTP) for accurate and reliable time synchronization (24).[cite: 4]
  * Use authenticated NTP to prevent malicious entities from tampering with your time synchronization.[cite: 4]
  * Configure a central time server within the entity (25).[cite: 4] This server should synchronize with a reliable external time source and then distribute the time to all other systems within the network.[cite: 4]
  * Use multiple time sources to avoid a single point of failure.[cite: 4]
  * Plan how time synchronization is handled across on-premises systems (for example servers in a company's own data centre), cloud services, and software-as-a-service (SaaS) platforms - especially if the organization uses a hybrid environment (a mix of on-premises and cloud-based systems).[cite: 4]
* Assets being logged should be marked as such in the asset inventory, in line with what is referred to in point 12.4 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Implement measures to protect log data against loss, including but not limited to redundant storage across multiple locations (e.g. cloud, secondary servers), retention of processed log events in structured systems and preservation of derived security insights (e.g. alerts, metrics) in line with what is referred to in point 4.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4] These complementary approaches ensure both data integrity and operational continuity in security monitoring and incident response.[cite: 4]
* Deploy separate tools to monitor the capacity and availability of the entity’s primary monitoring and logging systems.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Mechanisms for logs’ time synchronisation.[cite: 4]
* Mechanisms for logs’ redundant storage.[cite: 4]
* Logs from the activity of the tools that monitor the capacity and availability of the entity’s primary monitoring and logging systems.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procedures as well as the list of assets that are being logged shall be reviewed and, where appropriate, updated at regular intervals and after significant incidents.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Determine the frequency of reviews based on the risk assessment results related to the criticality of the assets, ensuring that reviews are conducted at least annually.[cite: 4]
* Include the testing of monitoring and logging procedures in security testing (section 6.5).[cite: 4]
* Review a random sample of logs to verify that all the assets that should be subject to the log are actually considered.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Review plans or schedules.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE TIPS

* In addition to the elements mentioned in point 3.2.3 of the Annex to the regulation, last login for every account should be logged.[cite: 4]
* Document monitoring and logging procedures.[cite: 4]
* Assess the frequency of monitoring activities to ensure they are sufficient to support risk-based security decisions for adequately protecting the entity’s network and information systems.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that personal data that are included in the logs is not processed unnecessarily.[cite: 4] When required, an additional level of protection is deployed after performing a data protection impact assessment.[cite: 4]
* Determine the log baselines in line with the needs and the capabilities of the business (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * structured or semi-structured, if possible, instead of unstructured format;[cite: 4]
  * consistent data format in line with the selected tools and well-known standards, for example JavaScript Object Notation and extensible markup language (XML);[cite: 4]
  * log level in line with the classification level of the asset being logged – the entity should assign a higher log level, for example ‘error’/‘fatal’, to highly classified assets while the lower log levels, for example ‘info’/‘debug’, should be used for assets with a lower classification; and[cite: 4]
  * the standard for the timestamps, for example ISO-8601 (26), RFC 3339 (27) or RFC 9557 (28).[cite: 4]
* Each log entry should contain necessary metadata such as (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * log level;[cite: 4]
  * timestamp;[cite: 4]
  * source identifier, for example the application or the device relevant to the entry; and[cite: 4]
  * a unique identifier for the entry.[cite: 4]
* Correlate data from different sources, if applicable.[cite: 4]
* Select tools that monitor and protect end point devices.[cite: 4]
* Select tools that can collect and analyse network traffic in real time to detect anomalies, data exfiltration and even the most advanced threats, while offering the option of automatic remediation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE (TIPS)

* Documented procedures.[cite: 4]
* Log baselines in place.[cite: 4]
* Logs (samples) containing necessary metadata.[cite: 4]
* EDR tools.[cite: 4]
* Network detection and response (NDR) tools.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall put in place a simple mechanism allowing their employees, suppliers and customers to report suspicious events.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Define what constitutes a suspicious event based on criteria (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * if the confidentiality or the integrity or the availability of the network or the information system has been affected;[cite: 4]
  * persistence, meaning whether the event is ongoing or not;[cite: 4]
  * impact, for example. the number of assets (potentially) affected; and[cite: 4]
  * compliance violation of a regulation or the entity’s policies.[cite: 4]
* Develop clear and concise guidelines for what information should be included in a report.[cite: 4] Align this information with the information that might be submitted to the CSIRT or, where applicable to the competent authority, if the event is notified in accordance with the NIS2 Directive Articles 23 or 30.[cite: 4] As good practice, the following should be reported as a minimum (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * date and time of the event,[cite: 4]
  * description of the event,[cite: 4]
  * any relevant screenshots, logs or other evidence,[cite: 4]
  * contact information for follow-up if necessary.[cite: 4]
* Provide multiple channels for reporting, such as email, a web form, a dedicated phone line or a mobile app.[cite: 4] Ensure that these channels are easily accessible and intuitive to use.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented mechanism that outlines the process for reporting security events.[cite: 4]
* Examples of templates for reporting (29).[cite: 4]
* Personnel aware of the mechanism and who to contact if they notice something suspicious.[cite: 4]
* Existence of multiple reporting channels such as email addresses, web forms, phone numbers or dedicated reporting portals.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall, where appropriate, communicate the event reporting mechanism to their suppliers and customers and shall regularly train their employees how to use the mechanism.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Make appropriate means for reporting available to personnel and the entity’s suppliers and customers.[cite: 4]
* Consider anonymous reporting to encourage individuals to report security events without fear of reprisal.[cite: 4]
* Take into account legal obligations to report an incident to the competent authorities (and CSIRTs) in line with the NIS2 Directive Articles 23 and 30, including any obligations about when the incident should be reported.[cite: 4]
* Regularly remind stakeholders of the reporting mechanism through email newsletters, posters and other communication channels.[cite: 4]
* Conduct regular exercises or simulations to test the effectiveness of the reporting mechanism.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Evidence of past communications and event reporting.[cite: 4]
* Documented procedures for communicating about events, describing (indicative, non-exhaustive list:
  * reasons/motivations for communicating or reporting (business reasons and legal reasons, etc.),[cite: 4]
  * the type of events in scope,[cite: 4]
  * the required content of communications,[cite: 4]
  * notifications or reports,[cite: 4]
  * the channels to be used and[cite: 4]
  * the roles responsible for communicating, notifying and reporting.[cite: 4]
* Training materials provided to employees, suppliers and customers regarding the reporting mechanism.[cite: 4]
* Periodic simulations and awareness raising activities to assess the readiness of personnel and the adequacy of the mechanism for reporting an event.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE TIPS

* Maintain a record of all reported events.[cite: 4]
* Ensure compliance with other relevant regulations and laws regarding data privacy, confidentiality and incident reporting.[cite: 4]
* Ask for legal advice, if necessary, to understand any legal implications of the reporting mechanism.[cite: 4]
* Evaluate past communications and reporting about events.[cite: 4]
* Review and update the reporting mechanism and the communication plans (Annex to the regulation, point 3.3), based on changes or past events.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE (TIPS)

* Record of events and, for each event, the impact, cause, actions taken and lessons learnt.[cite: 4]
* Summaries of previous reviews, if any.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall assess suspicious events to determine whether they constitute incidents and, if so, determine their nature and severity.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Use criteria to assess whether a suspicious event is an incident or not.[cite: 4] The guidance in section 3.1.2 provides an indicative, non-exhaustive list of such criteria.[cite: 4]
* Determine the nature and severity of the event based on a categorisation system referred to in point 3.1.2 (a) of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Defined criteria in place.[cite: 4]
* A categorisation system referred to in point 3.1.2 (a) of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of point 3.4.1, the relevant entities shall act in the following manner:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: carry out the assessment based on predefined criteria laid down in advance and on a triage to determine prioritisation of incident containment and eradication;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: assess the existence of recurring incidents as referred to in Article 4 of this Regulation on a quarterly basis;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: review the appropriate logs for the purposes of event assessment and classification;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: put in place a process for log correlation and analysis and[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: reassess and reclassify events in case of new information becoming available or after analysis of previously available information.[cite: 4]
