parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* In the procedures defined in points 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation, include activities for assessing suspicious events to determine their nature and severity.[cite: 4] These activities should include steps such as:[cite: 4]
  * gathering relevant information and evidence related to the event;[cite: 4]
  * analysing the potential impact on the entity’s systems, data and operations;[cite: 4]
  * determining the severity of the incident based on predefined criteria.[cite: 4]
* Implement playbooks (30) or runbooks to guide initial assessment actions for common types of incidents, for example ransomware, phishing, data or device loss, or fire.[cite: 4]
* Classify events based on their nature, severity and potential impact.[cite: 4] Common classifications may include:[cite: 4]
  * low, medium, high or critical severity;[cite: 4]
  * incident types (e.g. malicious software infection or unauthorized access);[cite: 4]
  * regulatory or compliance implications.[cite: 4]
* Prioritise the event according to specific criteria, as defined in the categorisation system included in the incident handling policy referred to in point 3.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* By performing root cause analysis (31), determine recurring instances (32) of an incident.[cite: 4]
  * Consider that the root cause of an incident may be challenging to determine during the early stages of incident handling, so the assessment of the existence of recurring incidents may be delayed.[cite: 4]
* Review and correlate the logs in line with what is referred to in point 3.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Assess past events and their classification to improve processes, procedures and thresholds.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented procedures or guidelines related to event assessment, including steps for gathering information, analysing impact and determining severity.[cite: 4]
* Existence of documented criteria or guidelines for prioritizing events based on severity and potential impact.[cite: 4]
* Existence of a process for triaging incoming alerts or reports of suspicious events.[cite: 4]
* Playbooks for common types of incidents.[cite: 4]
* Periodic reviews of assessment and classification of past events to improve processes, procedures and thresholds.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE TIPS

* Consider deploying SIEM, EDR, XDR or similar system that will allow and facilitate the correlation and analysis of data.[cite: 4]
* Where possible, utilise automation to triage incoming alerts and prioritise them based on severity and potential impact.[cite: 4]
* Integrate security events into the central SIEM or EDR/XDR solution, where available.[cite: 4]
* Take into account the confidentiality of the data stored, especially when correlating and analysing log files, by (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * minimising data collected, meaning only collecting and analysing logs that fit the purpose – avoid retaining unnecessary personal or sensitive data;[cite: 4]
  * anonymising or pseudonymising the collected data, when possible;[cite: 4]
  * applying good security practices where appropriate and relevant, such as access control, encryption, regular audits and monitoring;[cite: 4]
  * applying the data retention policy in alignment with GDPR requirements and regularly purging data that is no longer needed; and[cite: 4]
  * considering data protection and relevant legal and compliance obligations other than the NIS2 Directive.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE (TIPS)

* SIEM, EDR/XDR or similar system.[cite: 4]
* Tools supporting incident triage.[cite: 4]
* Measures to protect the security of information during log analysis and correlation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall respond to incidents in accordance with documented procedures and in a timely manner.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Establish a dedicated incident response team comprising employees with the necessary technical expertise and authority to respond effectively to incidents, where appropriate.[cite: 4]
* Define roles and responsibilities within the incident response team, such as incident coordinators, analysts and communication liaisons, where appropriate.[cite: 4]
* Take into account industry-recognised standards when developing the incident response procedures (33).[cite: 4]
* Implement playbooks or runbooks to guide incident response actions for common types of incidents.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Assignment of roles within the incident response team.[cite: 4]
* Documented standards and/or good practices that are taken into account.[cite: 4]
* Playbooks or incident response plans for common types of incidents.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The incident response procedures shall include the following stages:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: incident containment, to prevent the consequences of the incident from spreading;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: eradication, to prevent the incident from continuing or reappearing,[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: recovery from the incident, where necessary.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Create incident response procedures outlining the steps referred to in point 3.5.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Ensure that the handling of cybersecurity incidents takes into account the entity’s priorities and the impact of the incident.[cite: 4]
  * Recognize and address potential conflicts between the following objectives during incident handling:[cite: 4]
    * forensic activities – preserving and securing evidence for legal, compliance or investigative purposes;[cite: 4]
    * incident response activities – mitigating and removing current threats to prevent further damage; and[cite: 4]
    * operational continuity – minimizing disruption to IT services and maintaining critical operations.[cite: 4]
  * Where these objectives conflict, establish a clear decision-making process that:[cite: 4]
    * prioritises based on the accepted risk tolerance levels, business impact and legal obligations;[cite: 4]
    * involves coordination between cybersecurity, legal/compliance and operational teams; and[cite: 4]
    * documents the rationale for prioritisation decisions to ensure transparency and accountability.[cite: 4]
  * Develop incident response playbooks that incorporate decision making and escalation paths for managing trade-offs between evidence preservation, threat containment and operational continuity.[cite: 4]
* Keep the management bodies informed.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Procedures for incident response, including types of incidents that could occur, objectives, roles and responsibilities.[cite: 4]
* Detailed description, for each incident type, of how to manage the incident and when to escalate to management bodies (e.g. chief information security officer), etc.[cite: 4]
* Records from resolution of conflicting objectives during response to past incidents.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall establish communication plans and procedures:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: with the Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs) or, where applicable, the competent authorities, related to incident notification;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: with relevant internal and external stakeholders.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Ensure that the communication plan (Annex to the regulation, point 3.1.2) includes procedures for how to communicate the incident to the relevant authorities, the national CSIRT and internal and external stakeholders, including, where applicable, customers, direct suppliers, service providers and, if open source is used, contacts for free and open source software projects.[cite: 4]
* Include contact information for key personnel, external stakeholders and relevant authorities.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Procedures for how to communicate the incident to the relevant authorities and the CSIRT.[cite: 4]
* Procedures for how to communicate the incident to customers or how and when to involve a supplier (if applicable).[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall log incident response activities in accordance with the procedures referred to in point 3.2.1. and record evidence.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Log incident response information which contains (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * time of detection, containment and eradication;[cite: 4]
  * when the systems recovered;[cite: 4]
  * indicators of compromise;[cite: 4]
  * root cause;[cite: 4]
  * actions taken during each phase namely, detection, containment and eradication;[cite: 4]
  * assessment of the scope and the level of impact of the incident;[cite: 4]
  * communications when responding to the incident;[cite: 4]
  * post incident lessons learnt and recommendations; and[cite: 4]
  * whether the CSIRT or the competent authority was notified of the incident according to the NIS2 Directive Articles 23 and 30.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Logs from incident response.[cite: 4]
* Use of a system (e.g. SIEM, EDR/XDR or ticket system).[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall test at planned intervals their incident response procedures.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Test the entity’s incident response procedures at least annually.[cite: 4]
* Test different types of incidents, for example ransomware, phishing, data breach and DoS.[cite: 4]
* Ensure that test scenarios involve employees from different departments as well as external stakeholders, for example suppliers and service providers.[cite: 4]
  * Where necessary, include management bodies in the tests so that they understand their role during an incident.[cite: 4]
* Conduct post-test reviews for possible lessons learnt.[cite: 4]
* Update the incident response procedures based on the lessons learnt from the test, if applicable.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented plans or schedules for future incident response tests.[cite: 4]
* Records from tests of different types of incidents.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE TIPS

* Issue instructions on how to respond to the most common types of incidents (ransomware, phishing, data breach, DoS, etc.) including containment, eradication and recovery steps.[cite: 4]
* Include guidelines for preserving evidence and maintaining chain of custody to support forensic analysis and legal proceedings if necessary.[cite: 4]
* Consider the use of automated solutions for incident response, for example security orchestration, automation and response technologies or similar systems.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE (TIPS)

* Up-to-date incident response procedures based on tests conducted and/or change logs.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Where appropriate, the relevant entities shall carry out post-incident reviews after recovery from incidents.[cite: 4] The post-incident reviews shall identify, where possible, the root cause of the incident and result in documented lessons learned to reduce the occurrence and consequences of future incidents.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Conduct root cause analysis (34) and identify the root cause of the incident, where possible.[cite: 4]
* Identify contributing factors and areas for improvement in incident detection, response and recovery processes.[cite: 4]
* Investigate significant incidents and write final incident reports, including actions taken and recommendations to mitigate future occurrence of this type of incident.[cite: 4]
* Document lessons learnt, accompanied by recommendations and their owners, based on logs from incident response referred to in point 3.5.4 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Share any relevant findings in the post-incident review with affected stakeholders, for example suppliers, service providers, free and open source component maintainers.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Results of root cause analysis.[cite: 4]
* Individual reports of the handling of significant incidents.[cite: 4]
* Documented lessons learnt from incidents.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall ensure that post-incident reviews contribute to improving their approach to network and information security, to risk treatment measures and to incident handling, detection and response procedures.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Analyse the post-incident review findings to identify gaps and weaknesses in the entity’s network and information security status.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that the identified gaps and weaknesses feed back to the risk assessment and risk treatment plan (Annex to the regulation, point 2.1).[cite: 4]
* Assess whether existing risk treatment measures were effective in preventing or mitigating the incident.[cite: 4]
* Document the findings and lessons learnt from each post-incident review comprehensively.[cite: 4]
* Consider whether information security requirements have been met throughout the handling of a cybersecurity incident or whether measures may need to be taken to restore them (e.g. resetting passwords for emergency administrative access).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Post-incident review reports that detail findings, lessons learnt and recommendations for improvement following security incidents.[cite: 4]
* Analysis, resolution and mitigation measures taken, communicated to all relevant personnel.[cite: 4]
* Updated risk assessment and risk treatment plan, which includes findings of the post-incident reviews.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review at planned intervals if incidents led to post-incident reviews.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Conduct an annual review or a review after significant incidents, to determine if an incident has led to a post-incident review.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented plans or schedules for future reviews.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE TIPS

* Determine the composition of the review team, including members from relevant departments such as IT, security, legal and management bodies.[cite: 4]
* Review existing network and information security policies, topic-specific policies relevant to the incident, incident handling procedures and policy and incident response procedures in light of the lessons learnt from post-incident reviews.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE (TIPS)

* Minutes of the post-incident review team.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of updates to network and information security or topic-specific policies and procedures based on the lessons learnt from post-incident reviews.[cite: 4]

groups.title: 4.1 BUSINESS CONTINUITY AND DISASTER RECOVERY PLAN

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of Article 21(2), point (c) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the relevant entities shall lay down and maintain a business continuity and disaster recovery plan to apply in the case of incidents.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account industry-recognised standards when developing the business continuity (35) and disaster recovery plan.[cite: 4]
* Create a list of natural disasters (e.g. hurricane, fire, flooding) and other occurrences (e.g. human error) that could affect the services together with a list of disaster recovery capabilities (e.g. backups, tests, recovery objectives, etc.).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Business continuity plan.[cite: 4]
* Disaster recovery plan.[cite: 4]
* Business continuity and disaster recovery plans are in line with documented standards and/or good practices.[cite: 4]
* List of natural and/or major disasters that could affect the services and a list of disaster recovery capabilities (either those available internally or provided by third parties).[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities’ operations shall be restored according to the business continuity and disaster recovery plan.[cite: 4] The plan shall be based on the results of the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1 and shall include, where appropriate, the following:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: purpose, scope and audience;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: roles and responsibilities;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: key contacts and (internal and external) communication channels;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: conditions for plan activation and deactivation;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: order of recovery for operations;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: recovery plans for specific operations, including recovery objectives;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: required resources, including backups and redundancies;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: restoring and resuming activities from temporary measures.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Keep logs of activation and execution of the business continuity plan, including:[cite: 4]
  * decisions taken;[cite: 4]
  * steps followed; and[cite: 4]
  * final recovery time.[cite: 4]
* Determine the order of recovery based on criteria, including (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * the asset classification level;[cite: 4]
  * the importance of the service for the entity;[cite: 4]
  * dependencies (services or assets that are essential for others are restored first);[cite: 4]
  * recovery objectives (Annex to the regulation, point 4.1.3);[cite: 4]
  * resource availability; and[cite: 4]
  * regulatory requirements.[cite: 4]
* Conduct capacity planning so that necessary capacity for information processing, telecommunications and environmental support exists after business continuity plan activation.[cite: 4]
* Consider primary and alternate telecommunications service providers, section 13.1, to properly maintain disaster recovery plans (for the services provided).[cite: 4]
  * For remote work, employees handling critical operations should:[cite: 4]
    * have access to backup internet solutions (e.g. mobile broadband, tethering capabilities) and[cite: 4]
    * participate in regular testing of failover options, including VPN access and voice communications (e.g. VoIP or cloud telephony) over backup networks.[cite: 4]
* Prepare for recovery and restoration of services after a disaster by identifying measures such as:[cite: 4]
  * failover sites in other regions;[cite: 4]
  * backups of data with high criticality to remote locations; and[cite: 4]
  * tested restore procedures with regular validation cycles.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that third party services (e.g. hot site) will be available in case of disaster, where appropriate.[cite: 4]
* Implement advanced measures for disaster recovery capabilities, where appropriate, for example:[cite: 4]
  * full redundancy;[cite: 4]
  * failover mechanisms; and[cite: 4]
  * alternative site.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Measures in place for dealing with disasters, such as failover sites in other regions and backups of data to remote locations.[cite: 4]
* Up-to-date organisational structures widely communicated.[cite: 4]
* Inventory of sectors and services essential for and/or dependent on the continuity of the network and service operation, and contingency plans for mitigating the impact related to dependent and interdependent sectors and services.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall carry out a business impact analysis to assess the potential impact of severe disruptions to their business operations and shall, based on the results of the business impact analysis, establish continuity requirements for the network and information systems.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Based on the results of the BIA (36) and risk assessment, the entity should establish appropriate recovery objectives, referred to in point 4.1.2 (f) of the Annex to the regulation (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * Recovery time objectives (RTOs) to determine the maximum amount of time allowed for the recovery of business resources and functions (e.g. information and communications technology (ICT) systems and processes, respectively) after a disaster occurs, for example maximum downtime of the entity’s website, enterprise resource planning (ERP) system or email system.[cite: 4]
  * Recovery point objective (RPO) to determine how much data it is acceptable for specific ICT activities or applications to lose.[cite: 4] Typically, they are measured in maximum time needed to recover data without causing unacceptable, according to the risk assessment, damage to the entity’s activities, for example maximum recovery time for an e-commerce website, an ERP system or an email server.[cite: 4]
  * Service delivery objective (SDO) to determine the minimum level of performance that needs to be reached by business functions during the alternate processing mode.[cite: 4] An indicative and non-exhaustive list of examples includes:[cite: 4]
    * the percentage of inbound calls to be answered by a call centre within a specific timeframe;[cite: 4]
    * the level of availability of ordering and payment systems of an e-commerce website within a specific timeframe;[cite: 4]
    * the restoration time for accessing essential shared folders via a cloud file access system; and[cite: 4]
    * the timeframe within which the full functionality of the remote work infrastructure is restored.[cite: 4]
  * Maximum acceptable outage (MAO) or maximum tolerable period of disruption (MTPD) to determine the time it would take for the potential impacts of not providing a product/service or performing an activity to become unacceptable or significant, in accordance with the risk assessment.[cite: 4] Typically they are longer than RTOs.[cite: 4] MAOs focus on service availability while RPOs focus on data loss.[cite: 4] An indicative and non-exhaustive list of examples:[cite: 4]
    * the period of time beyond which the customer service would be severely impacted and reputation risk increases quickly;[cite: 4]
    * the longest period of time that extended outage of an e-commerce website might result to major loss of sales and customer trust;[cite: 4]
    * the longest period of time that shared access to project files may halt collaboration or decision-making in case that data is stored in cloud; and[cite: 4]
    * the maximum acceptable outage for remote work infrastructure beyond which business functions are significantly impaired and productivity losses begin to escalate.[cite: 4]
* RTOs, RPOs and SDOs may be used to determine backup and redundancy procedures.[cite: 4]
* Document disaster recovery plan, taking into account:[cite: 4]
  * the RTOs, RPOs and SDOs; and[cite: 4]
  * compliance with applicable regulations and legislation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented BIA with specific recovery objectives.[cite: 4]
* Processes, procedures and measures to ensure the required level of continuity in disruptive situations.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The business continuity plan and disaster recovery plan shall be tested, reviewed and, where appropriate, updated at planned intervals and following significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks.[cite: 4] The relevant entities shall ensure that the plans incorporate lessons learnt from such tests.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Test, review and, if necessary, update the business continuity and disaster recovery plans at least annually.[cite: 4]
* Choose and combine method(s) to test the business continuity and disaster recovery plans, such as:[cite: 4]
  * alternative locations for personnel;[cite: 4]
  * disaster recovery locations – hot sites;[cite: 4]
  * digital twins;[cite: 4]
  * simulations;[cite: 4]
  * table top exercises.[cite: 4]
* Test business continuity and disaster recovery plans regularly, taking into account:[cite: 4]
  * change logs;[cite: 4]
  * past incidents; and[cite: 4]
  * results of previous tests.[cite: 4]
* Where appropriate, test the disaster recovery plan at an alternate processing site to:[cite: 4]
  * familiarize related personnel with the facility and available resources; and[cite: 4]
  * evaluate the capabilities of the alternate processing site to support operations.[cite: 4]
* Test data centre infrastructure for:[cite: 4]
  * availability;[cite: 4]
  * auto failover;[cite: 4]
  * power failover between power providers and/or power provider to backup (for example generators or batteries); and[cite: 4]
  * resilience to maintain service to customers.[cite: 4]
* Define full recovery and reconstitution of the information system to a known state as part of the disaster recovery plan testing.[cite: 4]
* Update business continuity and disaster recovery plans and related measures based on:[cite: 4]
  * change logs;[cite: 4]
  * past incidents;[cite: 4]
  * documented results of the continuity of operations test activities; and[cite: 4]
  * records of individual training activities.[cite: 4]
* Review change logs and documented results from past tests on business continuity and disaster recovery plans to ensure that the plans incorporate lessons learnt from such tests.[cite: 4]
* Review and, if necessary, update roles and responsibilities.[cite: 4]
* Review dependent third parties’ disaster recovery plans to ensure that the plans meet entity’s business continuity requirements.[cite: 4]
* Communicate changes to business continuity and disaster recovery plans to related key personnel.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented plans or schedules for future tests.[cite: 4]
* Records from previous tests, reviews and possible updates.[cite: 4]
* Logs of activation and execution of business continuity and disaster recovery plans, including decisions taken, steps followed and final recovery time.[cite: 4]
* Communications, for example emails, documents and intranet announcements, concerning changes to the business continuity and disaster recovery plans.[cite: 4]
* Evidences that lessons learnt from past tests are incorporated into the plans, for example workflow changes and updated plans.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall maintain backup copies of data and provide sufficient available resources, including facilities, network and information systems and staff, to ensure an appropriate level of redundancy.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Consider whether to invest in own redundancy or to engage third parties, for example cloud providers, to provide such redundancy, in alignment with the BIA (Annex to the regulation, point 4.1.3).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Backups are physically separated from the systems that generated them.[cite: 4]
* If the service is offered by a third party, SLAs.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the results of the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1 and the business continuity plan, the relevant entities shall lay down backup plans which include the following:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: recovery times;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: assurance that backup copies are complete and accurate, including configuration data and data stored in cloud computing service environment;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: storing backup copies (online or offline) in a safe location or locations, which are not in the same network as the system and are at sufficient distance to escape any damage from a disaster at the main site;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: appropriate physical and logical access controls to backup copies, in accordance with the asset classification level;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: restoring data from backup copies;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: retention periods based on business and regulatory requirements.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Recovery times should not exceed the recovery objectives referred to in 4.1.2 (f) of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Concerning retention periods consider what is referred to in point 3.2.5 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* If an entity engages third parties to ensure an appropriate level of redundancy, it should be clearly decided whether it is the entity's responsibility to compile the backup plans or if the third parties have any involvement in the process.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Backup plans.[cite: 4]
* Logs from backup software that show regular backups are being performed.[cite: 4]
* Backups physically separated and with an appropriate level of protection, including encryption.[cite: 4]
* Logs or reports confirming that one copy of the backup is stored off-site, such as in a cloud storage service or a remote data centre.[cite: 4]
* Configuration settings of backup software to verify that it is set up to create copies of data and store them on different media.[cite: 4]
* Clear and concise restoration procedures that cover all relevant systems and services.[cite: 4]
* If applicable, settings of the cloud storage service to ensure it is configured to receive and store backup copies.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall perform regular integrity checks on the backup copies.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Check the integrity of the backup copies.[cite: 4] An indicative, non-exhaustive list of good practices is the following:[cite: 4]
  * use checksums or hashing algorithms to verify that the data in your backups matches the original data (section 9.2);[cite: 4]
  * implement automated scripts to run these checks regularly, reducing the risk of human error;[cite: 4]
  * schedule regular tests to restore data from backups to ensure they are complete, functional and validated by business users to confirm the accuracy and usability of the restored data;[cite: 4]
  * test various recovery scenarios, including full system restores and individual file recoveries, to ensure all aspects of your backup system are reliable; and[cite: 4]
  * consider using cloud storage solutions for off-site backups, which often include built-in integrity checks and redundancy.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Logs or reports showing that checksum or hashing algorithms are used.[cite: 4]
* Settings in backup software or scripts that specify the use of checksums or hashing algorithms.[cite: 4]
* Records of regular tests in which data is restored from backups.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of tests of different recovery scenarios, including full system restores and individual file recoveries.[cite: 4]
* Logs or reports from actual incidents in which recovery procedures were implemented (Annex to the regulation, points 3.2 and 3.5).[cite: 4]
* If the service is offered by a third party, SLAs.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the results of the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1 and the business continuity plan, the relevant entities shall ensure sufficient availability of resources by at least partial redundancy of the following:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: network and information systems;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: assets, including facilities, equipment and supplies;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: personnel with the necessary responsibility, authority and competence;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: appropriate communication channels.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Define minimum resources needed to ensure at least partial redundancy for each of points (a), (b), (c) and (d).[cite: 4] These may include the following:[cite: 4]
  * network and information systems: one or more of the following (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
    * multiple internet service providers,[cite: 4]
    * load balancing,[cite: 4]
    * mirrored servers,[cite: 4]
    * virtualisation,[cite: 4]
    * redundant array of independent disks;[cite: 4]
  * assets: one or more of the following (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
    * shared workspaces,[cite: 4]
    * backup locations,[cite: 4]
    * spare equipment,[cite: 4]
    * multiple suppliers for the same categories of products;[cite: 4]
  * personnel: one or more of the following (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
    * job rotation,[cite: 4]
    * backup assignments,[cite: 4]
    * emergency drills;[cite: 4]
  * multiple communication platforms, for example social media, messaging apps and email; and[cite: 4]
  * multiple methods to power a site, either through multiple electrical providers or with a combination of electrical providers and backup mechanisms, such as generators.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* One or more of the above mechanisms are in place.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Where appropriate, the relevant entities shall ensure that monitoring and adjustment of resources, including facilities, systems and personnel, is duly informed by backup and redundancy requirements.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Decisions about resource allocation and adjustments should be guided by the need for backups and redundancy.[cite: 4] To this end, the entity might consider one or more of the following (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * prioritisation of resources based on the results of the risk analysis;[cite: 4]
  * partial redundancy;[cite: 4]
  * diverse backup locations; and[cite: 4]
  * continuous monitoring of the resources where redundancy is necessary.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Evidence of elements referred to in point 4.2.4 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Evidence from periodic simulations and awareness raising activities to assess the readiness of personnel and the adequacy of the procedures.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall carry out regular testing of the recovery of backup copies and redundancies to ensure that, in recovery conditions, they can be relied upon and cover the copies, processes and knowledge to perform an effective recovery.[cite: 4] The relevant entities shall document the results of the tests and, where needed, take corrective action.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Tailor the frequency of the backup checks to the data criticality based on the risk assessment (section 2.1).[cite: 4] As an example:[cite: 4]
  * Data with high criticality might be checked on a weekly basis.[cite: 4]
  * Data with moderate and low criticality might be checked on a monthly basis.[cite: 4]
  * Significant changes should be checked immediately after the change.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that the issues and lessons learnt from exercises are addressed by the responsible people and that the relevant processes and systems are updated accordingly.[cite: 4]
* Involve suppliers and other third parties, such as business partners or customers in tests.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Reports/logs of regular testing of backup status, processes and procedures.[cite: 4]
* Test programme for backup plans, including types of contingencies, frequency, roles and responsibilities, templates and procedures for conducting tests, and templates for post-test reports.[cite: 4]
* Reports of past tests of backup and contingency plans.[cite: 4]
* Reports about tests and drills showing the execution of the plans, including evidence that recovery times were met and lessons learnt from the tests.[cite: 4]
* Issues and lessons learnt from past tests addressed by the responsible people.[cite: 4]
* Updated test plans, review comments and/or change logs.[cite: 4]
* Input from suppliers and other third parties involved about how to improve test scenarios.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall put in place a process for crisis management.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account industry-recognised standards when developing the crisis management process (38).[cite: 4]
  * Be aware that each crisis may be different and further analysis may be required on an ad hoc basis.[cite: 4]
  * Consider the various aspects (e.g. technical, operational, communication and remediation) of crisis management, including processes, roles and responsibilities.[cite: 4]
* Because the escalation of an incident to crisis status depends on an entity’s risk appetite and incident handling capabilities, the entity should define criteria on when a crisis is declared (39).[cite: 4] This may refer to incidents that cause serious impact, beyond a certain threshold of tolerance.[cite: 4] These criteria may include the following (indicative and non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * the incident poses significant risk to critical assets or operations with high criticality, for example high-severity incidents (e.g. data breaches involving sensitive information);[cite: 4]
  * the incident disrupts business operations significantly, for example prolonged downtime, widespread loss of services or significant impact on customer service;[cite: 4]
  * the breadth of the incident, that is, whether it affects multiple systems, departments or geographic locations, indicating a wider threat;[cite: 4]
  * the potential impact on the entity’s reputation – incidents that could lead to public scrutiny or loss of customer trust should be escalated;[cite: 4]
  * the potential impact of the cybersecurity incident on the confidentiality, integrity, authenticity and availability of data;[cite: 4]
  * the sophistication and motivations of the threat actors involved.[cite: 4] Incidents linked to advanced persistent threats or organised cybercrime may require a higher-level response, beyond the capabilities of the entity;[cite: 4]
  * the potential to escalate further (e.g. if vulnerabilities could be exploited again or if malware is spreading).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Crisis management process is in line with documented standards and/or good practices.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall ensure that the crisis management process addresses at least the following elements:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: roles and responsibilities for personnel and, where appropriate, suppliers and service providers, specifying the allocation of roles in crisis situations, including specific steps to follow;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: appropriate communication means between the relevant entities and relevant competent authorities;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: application of appropriate measures to ensure the maintenance of network and information system security in crisis situations.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of point (b), the flow of information between the relevant entities and relevant competent authorities shall include both obligatory communications, such as incident reports and related timelines and non-obligatory communications.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* For crisis communication, consider (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * legal obligations for communication, such as timing of communication, in particular referring to requirements for notification;[cite: 4]
  * how information will be disseminated to internal and external stakeholders (employees, customers, direct suppliers and service providers, emergency services, etc.) during a crisis;[cite: 4]
  * templates for communication;[cite: 4]
  * communication channels to be used for each type of stakeholder, considering that:[cite: 4]
    * internal and external stakeholders may use different communication channels;[cite: 4]
    * normal communication channels might not be safe in crisis mode;[cite: 4]
    * channels used to notify and communicate with competent authorities should also be indicated;[cite: 4]
  * up-to-date contact information for internal and external stakeholders.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented crisis management process.[cite: 4]
* List of members of the crisis management team, including their roles, contact information and alternatives.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall implement a process for managing and making use of information received from the CSIRTs or, where applicable, the competent authorities, concerning incidents, vulnerabilities, threats or possible mitigation measures.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Implement a process for managing and making use of information received from the CSIRTs.[cite: 4] Consider the following steps (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * designate a point of contact with the CSIRT;[cite: 4]
  * ensure that the point of contact has sufficient knowledge concerning incidents and threat intelligence.[cite: 4]
  * classify incoming information into categories such as incidents, vulnerabilities, threats and mitigation measures.[cite: 4]
  * assign priority levels based on severity and potential impact on the entity, if the information is relevant or applicable[cite: 4]
  * have the CSIRT contact point review the information for relevance and urgency.[cite: 4]
  * validate information against internal logs, threat intelligence feeds and existing security policies.[cite: 4]
  * for vulnerabilities and threats, if applicable, collaborate with relevant teams (IT, security, operations) to develop a mitigation strategy;[cite: 4]
  * update or create incident response plans based on the nature of the threats or incidents reported in accordance with point 3.5 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
  * where appropriate, implement the mitigation measures and communicate with the relevant stakeholders in accordance with point 3.5 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
  * share insights and feedback on incidents and mitigations with the CSIRT on a voluntary basis.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Previous communications with CSIRTs or, where applicable, the competent authorities, for example emails, correspondence and meeting minutes.[cite: 4]
* Evidences that the point of contact has sufficient knowledge concerning incidents and threat intelligence.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall test, review and, where appropriate, update the crisis management plan on a regular basis or following significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Test the crisis management process annually.[cite: 4]
* Test the crisis management process through, for example, an exercise or simulation, by (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * taking into account past crisis situations;[cite: 4]
  * comparing the results of the tests to the objectives defined, for instance the recovery objectives in point 4.1.2 (f) of the Annex to the regulation (e.g. RTOs, RPOs and SDOs); and[cite: 4]
  * using the results of the comparison to update and improve the crisis management procedure.[cite: 4]
* Review and update, if necessary, the crisis management process after a test or following significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks.[cite: 4]
* Review and update the policy on the security of network and information systems and crisis management organisational measures after a test or following significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documentation showing how crisis management integrates with the entity’s incident response plans (Annex to the regulation, point 3.5), particularly for ICT-related incidents.[cite: 4]
* Documents identifying any previous crises and assessing their likelihood of recurrence and potential impact on business operations.[cite: 4]
* Documentation of previous crisis management tests, including the scenarios tested, participants involved and outcomes.[cite: 4]
* After-action reports or evaluations from crisis management tests, identifying strengths, weaknesses and areas for improvement.[cite: 4]
* Records of internal or external reviews and audits of the crisis management plan, including any findings and corrective actions taken.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of Article 21(2), point (d) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the relevant entities shall establish, implement and apply a supply chain security policy which governs the relations with their direct suppliers and service providers to mitigate the identified risks to the security of network and information systems.[cite: 4] In the supply chain security policy, the relevant entities shall identify their role in the supply chain and communicate it to their direct suppliers and service providers.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account industry-recognised standards or good practices when developing the supply chain policy (40).[cite: 4]
* The role of a supplier or service provider might be one or more of the following (41):[cite: 4]
  * ICT supplier (including software and hardware supplier),[cite: 4]
  * Manufacturer,[cite: 4]
  * managed service provider,[cite: 4]
  * managed security service provider and[cite: 4]
  * cloud computing provider.[cite: 4]
* In the case of free and open source software (FOSS), communities and projects that openly develop, maintain and distribute software may not be considered direct suppliers or service providers where no contractual relationship exists between the relevant entity and the open source project, beyond adherence to a standardised copyright licence, or where the contractual relationship is with an open source software steward (Regulation 2024/2847, Article 3(14) ‘provides support on a sustained basis for the development and ensures the viability of those products’).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Supply chain security policy in place and is in line with industry-recognised standards and/or good practices.[cite: 4]
* Evidence (e.g. email, contract or announcements) of the communication of the role of the entity to the direct suppliers and service providers, where possible.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: As part of the supply chain security policy referred to in point 5.1.1, the relevant entities shall lay down criteria to select and contract suppliers and service providers.[cite: 4] Those criteria shall include the following:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the cybersecurity practices of the suppliers and service providers, including their secure development procedures;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the ability of the suppliers and service providers to meet cybersecurity specifications set by the relevant entities;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the overall quality and resilience of ICT products and ICT services and the cybersecurity risk-management measures embedded in them, including the risks and classification level of the ICT products and ICT services;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the ability of the relevant entities to diversify sources of supply and limit vendor lock-in, where applicable.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Consider criteria such as:[cite: 4]
  * the legal jurisdiction ofходе the supplier or service provider, for example whether the supplier is regulated under the NIS2 Directive or the Cyber Resilience Act and in which jurisdiction(s);[cite: 4]
  * if available, compliance statements from the supplier in relation to the NIS2 Directive;[cite: 4]
  * the corporate ownership of the supplier or service provider;[cite: 4]
  * the supplier’s or service provider’s ability to ensure supply (e.g. size, reliance on other suppliers or service providers and degree of control over its own supply chain);[cite: 4]
  * the cybersecurity practices of the supplier or service provider, and whether adequate prioritisation is given to cybersecurity practices, attested by:[cite: 4]
    * industry standard certifications for cybersecurity;[cite: 4]
    * vendor risk-management software reports or other provider assessment reports (e.g. Standardized Information Gathering, vendor security assessment or consensus assessment initiative questionnaire), if available;[cite: 4]
  * notices or advice issued by national authorities on the selection of suppliers or service providers, if available;[cite: 4]
  * the sensitivity of the use of the products and services acquired;[cite: 4]
  * the supplier or service provider’s history in relation to cybersecurity events and breaches;[cite: 4]
  * the possibility of vendor lock-in, if the supplier or service provider is selected.[cite: 4] Parameters to consider are the use of open and interoperable standards, the use of open data formats, existing contracts with the supplier or service provider, the use of proprietary software features, etc.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* A policy containing the elements referred to in point 5.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When establishing their supply chain security policy, relevant entities shall take into account the results of the coordinated security risk assessments of critical supply chains carried out in accordance with Article 22(1) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, where applicable.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account any recommendations or guidance on supply chain security, published by the NIS Cooperation Group, established by the NIS2 Directive, Article 14 (42) and by the national competent authorities.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Evidence that scenarios and the recommendations of the NIS Cooperation Group have been taken into account in the supply chain policy, relevant to the entity’s business objectives.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Based on the supply chain security policy and taking into account the results of the risk assessment carried out in accordance with point 2.1. of this Annex, the relevant entities shall ensure that their contracts with the suppliers and service providers specify, where appropriate through service level agreements, the following, where appropriate:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: cybersecurity requirements for the suppliers or service providers, including requirements as regards the security in acquisition of ICT services or ICT products set out in point 6.1.;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: requirements regarding awareness, skills and training and where appropriate certifications, required from the suppliers’ or service providers’ employees;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: requirements regarding the verification of the background of the suppliers’ and service providers’ employees;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: an obligation on suppliers and service providers to notify, without undue delay, the relevant entities of incidents that present a risk to the security of the network and information systems of those entities;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the right to audit or right to receive audit reports;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: an obligation on suppliers and service providers to handle vulnerabilities that present a risk to the security of the network and information systems of the relevant entities;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: requirements regarding subcontracting and, where the relevant entities allow subcontracting, cybersecurity requirements for subcontractors in accordance with the cybersecurity requirements referred to in point (a);[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: obligations on the suppliers and service providers at the termination of the contract, such as retrieval and disposal of the information obtained by the suppliers and service providers in the exercise of their tasks.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Ensure that, in all relevant new and renewed contracts, the requirements from point 5.1.4 of the Annex to the regulation are included.[cite: 4]
* When dealing with large suppliers and service providers consider one or more of the following measures (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * collective bargaining by teaming up with similar size organisations for purchasing products or services in bulk;[cite: 4]
  * representation by an association of which the entity is a member of;[cite: 4]
  * legal advice for reviewing and negotiating a contract;[cite: 4]
  * negotiating specific clauses such as exit, pricing and SLAs (43);[cite: 4]
  * suppliers that publicly publish their security, privacy or reliability commitments;[cite: 4]
  * providers with standard certifications (e.g. ISO 27001, SOC 2);[cite: 4]
  * trusted platforms or marketplaces that vet suppliers (e.g. app stores, SaaS directories, partner networks);[cite: 4]
  * contract templates or free legal checklists from small business associations, NGOs or government sites;[cite: 4]
  * tools/services that allow easy data export, monthly payments or no lock-in;[cite: 4]
  * avoiding long-term commitments or vendor lock-in without clear exit strategies; and[cite: 4]
  * a short list of alternatives in case the supplier becomes unavailable.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Contracts that contain the elements referred to in point 5.1.4 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall take into account the elements referred to in point 5.1.2 and 5.1.3. as part of the selection process of new suppliers and service providers, as well as part of the procurement process referred to in point 6.1.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Perform a risk analysis before entering into any agreement with suppliers and service providers related to information security, taking into account the elements referred to in point 5.1.2 and 5.1.3, where appropriate (44).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Evidence that contracts with new suppliers and service providers or the procurement guidelines take into account the elements referred to in points 5.1.2 and 5.1.3.[cite: 4]
* Comparison between selected contracts and the associated tenders to check whether the secure acquisition of ICT systems, products and service processes and particularly the elements referred to in point 6.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation, are taken into consideration.[cite: 4]
* Risk analysis results from supplier and service provider evaluations.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review the supply chain security policy and monitor, evaluate and, where necessary, act upon changes in the cybersecurity practices of suppliers and service providers, at planned intervals and when significant changes to operations or risks or significant incidents related to the provision of ICT services or having impact on the security of the ICT products from suppliers and service providers occur.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review the supply chain policy at least annually.[cite: 4]
* Create and maintain a process to monitor suppliers and service providers over the life cycle.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Supply chain policy review plans or schedules.[cite: 4]
* Records from previous reviews.[cite: 4]
* List of security incidents related to or caused by engagement with a supplier or service provider.[cite: 4]
* Evidence that the policy was reviewed and possibly updated, after significant changes to operations or risks or significant incidents related to the provision of ICT services or having an impact on the security of the ICT products from suppliers and service providers.[cite: 4]
* Evidence from evaluations of suppliers and service providers.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of point 5.1.6., the relevant entities shall:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: regularly monitor reports on the implementation of the service level agreements, where applicable;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: review incidents related to ICT products and ICT services from suppliers and service providers;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: assess the need for unscheduled reviews and document the findings in a comprehensible manner;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: analyse the risks presented by changes related to ICT products and ICT services from suppliers and service providers and, where appropriate, take mitigating measures in a timely manner.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Set up a regular review (e.g. as part of a regular supplier meeting) and follow up on deviations from the agreed SLAs.[cite: 4]
* Define and assign responsibilities regarding maintenance, operation and ownership of assets.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that monitoring encompasses periodic reassessment of supplier and service provider compliance, and monitor supplier and service provider release notes.[cite: 4]
* Periodically ensure that product configuration is aligned with vendor recommendations, with increasing frequency as products age.[cite: 4]
* Keep track of security incidents related to or caused by suppliers and service providers as they might trigger an unscheduled review of the suppliers and service providers.[cite: 4] Other circumstances for such an unscheduled review include to suppliers and service providers (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * material changes in their operations;[cite: 4]
  * changes in their risk exposure;[cite: 4]
  * failure to meet their contractual obligations; and[cite: 4]
  * emergence of new threats or vulnerabilities affecting the provided ICT products or services.[cite: 4]
* Monitoring frequency should be aligned with supply chain policy (Annex to the regulation, point 5.1.1) and the review of the secure acquisition of ICT services, systems or products processes (Annex to the regulation, point 6.1.3).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Records showing that service levels are monitored in accordance with established SLA).[cite: 4]
* Incident response records which confirm whether the entity takes into account incidents related to ICT services, systems or products from suppliers and service providers;[cite: 4]
* Evidence that signed contracts with third parties (e.g. contractors and suppliers) are in line with the policy on the security of network and information systems, for example contractual clauses, references to key security-relevant roles and responsibilities, and requirements for the contractor to report incidents.[cite: 4]
* Supplier and service provider exit process, meaning documentation outlining how the entity manages the exit of suppliers and service providers.[cite: 4] This includes transitioning services, data and access rights when terminating a supplier and service provider relationship.[cite: 4]
* List of security incidents related to or caused by engagement with third parties.[cite: 4]

groups.title: 5.2 DIRECTORY OF SUPPLIERS AND SERVICE PROVIDERS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall maintain and keep up to date a registry of their direct suppliers and service providers, including:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: contact points for each direct supplier and service provider;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: a list of ICT products, ICT services and ICT processes provided by the direct supplier or service provider to the relevant entities.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Keep the registry up to date to ensure all information is current and accurate, that is, add, update and remove suppliers and service provider from the registry in the event of changes.[cite: 4]
* Conduct reviews of the registry, at least annually or when significant changes occur to ensure all information is current and accurate.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Registry of direct suppliers and service providers.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of registry updates following direct supplier and service provider changes.[cite: 4]
* Review plans or schedules.[cite: 4]

groups.title: 6. SECURITY IN NETWORK AND INFORMATION SYSTEMS ACQUISITION, DEVELOPMENT AND MAINTENANCE
6.1 SECURITY IN ACQUISITION OF ICT SERVICES OR ICT PRODUCTS

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of Article 21(2), point (e) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the relevant entities shall set and implement processes to manage risks stemming from the acquisition of ICT services or ICT products for components that are critical for the relevant entities’ security of network and information systems, based on the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1, from suppliers or service providers throughout their life cycle.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Integrate cybersecurity as a permanent component of the purchase process by dedicating a specific section to addressing it.[cite: 4] This includes any acquisition processes for selecting FOSS (48).[cite: 4]
* Document the process for secure acquisition of ICT services, systems or products and describe relevant procedures that support the process.[cite: 4]
* Take into account industry-recognised standards when developing the process (49).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Tender templates for the acquisition of ICT services, systems or products which address cybersecurity.[cite: 4]
* Documented process which is based on relevant standards and good practices.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of point 6.1.1., the processes referred to in point 6.1.1. shall include:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: security requirements to apply to the ICT services or ICT products to be acquired;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: requirements regarding security updates throughout the entire lifetime of the ICT services or ICT products or replacement after the end of the support period;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: information describing the hardware and software components used in the ICT services or ICT products;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: information describing the implemented cybersecurity functions of the ICT services or ICT products and the configuration required for their secure operation;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: assurance that the ICT services or ICT products comply with the security requirements according to point (a);[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: methods for validating that the delivered ICT services or ICT products are compliant to the stated security requirements, as well as documentation of the results of the validation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* The security requirements must include at least the means to detect, monitor and protect against unauthorized changes of software and information.[cite: 4]
* Ensure that support contracts cover the system life cycle and obsolescence management requirements, including the date until which the system must be supported and include continuous alerting.[cite: 4]
* Favour vendors that provide clear end-of-life information and that plan to provide separate critical security fixes.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that tenders request that suppliers or service providers provide tested solutions for security issues in legacy or new technologies free of charge and as soon as a relevant security issue becomes known.[cite: 4]
* Consider also the following information describing implemented cybersecurity functions such as (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * the potential risks that could arise from acquiring the specific ICT service, system or product.[cite: 4] This might involve penetration testing to identify threats, vulnerabilities and the potential impact on the entity’s operations;[cite: 4]
  * potential security tools that already need to be in place, for example a firewall, an intrusion detection system, a SIEM or a EDR/XDR;[cite: 4]
  * a specific security mechanism that might need to be in place, such as a specific encryption algorithm or a particular access control mechanism (e.g. MFA);[cite: 4]
  * cybersecurity standards for the ICT service, system or product that the entity needs to comply with;[cite: 4]
  * where appropriate, the required assurance level of the ICT product, system or service and the existence of a relevant certificate following the European Cybersecurity Scheme for ICT products based on Common Criteria (EUCC).[cite: 4]
* Consider evaluating the security of an ICT service, system or product before acquisition (50).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Past or ongoing tenders for acquiring ICT services, systems or products, that address cybersecurity by referring, as a minimum, to the elements outlined in point 6.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Comparison between selected contracts and the associated tenders to check whether the supply chain policy and particularly the elements referred to in points 5.1.4 and 5.1.5 of the Annex to the regulation, are taken into consideration.[cite: 4]
* Records from security tests before acquiring an ICT system or product.[cite: 4]
* Certificates, test reports or other supporting information for the ICT products or systems from suitably accredited conformity assessment bodies.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where appropriate, update the processes at planned intervals and when significant incidents occur.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review the processes for secure acquisition of ICT services, systems or products, and the procedures based on them, at least annually.[cite: 4]
* Review logs or records of all changes made to the processes for secure acquisition of ICT services, systems or products, and the procedures based on them, including details of the changes, approvals and implementation dates.[cite: 4]
* Align the tenders and contracts with the entity’s supply chain security policy (Annex to the regulation, point 5.1).[cite: 4]
* For ICT services, systems or products that are not provided by a supplier (e.g. open source projects), entities should share relevant results from internal assessments with them.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Review plans or schedules for processes for secure acquisition of ICT services, systems or products, and the procedures based on them.[cite: 4]
* Minutes from reviews or possible changes made to the processes for ICT services, system or product acquisition, and the procedures based on them, including actions taken to enhance security in future acquisitions.[cite: 4]
* Documented results of possible auditing activities, indicating compliance with internal secure acquisition of ICT services, systems or products processes and external regulations.[cite: 4]
* Change management records of changes made to the processes for secure acquisition of ICT services, systems or products, and the procedures based on them, including documentation of the review and approval process.[cite: 4]
* Incident response records that confirm whether the entity takes into account significant incidents when reviewing and updating the processes and procedures for secure acquisition of ICT services, systems or products.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: Before developing a network and information system, including software, the relevant entities shall lay down rules for the secure development of network and information systems and apply them when developing network and information systems in-house or when outsourcing the development of network and information systems.[cite: 4] The rules shall cover all development phases, including specification, design, development, implementation and testing.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account the entity’s policies and norms (if available) and industry-recognised standards when developing the rules for the secure development of network and information systems (51).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented rules for the secure development of network and information systems which align with the entity’s policies and norms and are based on relevant standards and good practices.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of point 6.2.1., the relevant entities shall:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: carry out an analysis of security requirements at the specification and design phases of any development or acquisition project undertaken by the relevant entities or on behalf of those entities;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: apply principles for engineering secure systems and secure coding principles to any information system development activities such as promoting cybersecurity-by-design, zero-trust architectures;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: lay down security requirements regarding development environments;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: establish and implement security testing processes in the development life cycle;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: appropriately select, protect and manage security test data;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: sanitise and anonymise testing data according to the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* A secure software development life cycle (SSDLC) process should be implemented by all entities.[cite: 4] However, smaller entities can use a less demanding process such as implementing secure-by-design practices and security-testing processes.[cite: 4]
* Depending on the type of requirement, the rules for the secure development of software and systems should include appropriate software testing methods (e.g. black-box, ad-hoc testing, static versus dynamic application security testing).[cite: 4]
* Test security by design at various stages of the secure development of the SSDLC prior to go-live, utilising independent tools and a self-service testing platform throughout the SSDLC.[cite: 4]
* When real production data - or derived variations of it - is used for testing, ensure that such data is properly sanitised or anonymised.[cite: 4] An indicative, non-exhaustive list of techniques:[cite: 4]
  * masking or pseudonymization on fields like names, emails, IDs;[cite: 4]
  * deletion or redaction of identifiers (e.g. personal IDs, birth dates, ZIP codes); and[cite: 4]
  * non-irreversible or one-way anonymisation.[cite: 4]
* When using Free and Open Source Software components, entities should take into account the voluntary nature of open source projects (see guidance of section 5.1).[cite: 4] Where possible, entities should assist the open source projects that they depend on in adopting secure systems and secure coding principles (such as introducing SSDLC processes suited to the project’s way of working).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Evidence that secure development rules have been adopted (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * documentation for each phase of the life cycle,[cite: 4]
  * process and workflow diagrams,[cite: 4]
  * audit and testing reports,[cite: 4]
  * version control,[cite: 4]
  * change management logs,[cite: 4]
  * code reviews, and[cite: 4]
  * project management tools.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of the test results from secure development environments, including that measures for protecting test data are maintained.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of the software-testing methods chosen for a particular test scenario and an explanation of the choice.[cite: 4]
* Test results of each phase of the SSDLC maintained and up to date.[cite: 4]
* Test results maintained and, where appropriate, approved by management bodies.[cite: 4]
* Evidence that a software-testing method is chosen at each stage of the software development life cycle.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For outsourced development of network and information systems, the relevant entities shall also apply the policies and procedures referred to in points 5 and 6.1.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Align the secure development rules with the security testing policy (Annex to the regulation, point 6.5) and procedures and with the secure acquisition of ICT services, systems or product processes (Annex to the regulation, point 6.1).[cite: 4]
* Communicate the internal development rules with the relevant personnel from outsourced development.[cite: 4]
* Hold regular cross-organisational unit meetings during all phases of the development life cycle.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Comparison of the secure development rules with the security-testing policy and with the secure acquisition of ICT services, systems or product processes, checking whether the security requirements are set consistently in all these documents.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of communicating the internal development rules with relevant personnel from outsourced development.[cite: 4]
* Records or minutes from cross organisational unit meetings where the development of a network and information system, including software, was discussed.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where necessary, update their secure development rules at planned intervals.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review the rules for the secure development of network and information systems at least once every two years.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documentation that outlines the schedule and frequency for reviewing secure development rules.[cite: 4]
* Documented evidence of the process for reviewing the patch development process and secure-by design software configurations.[cite: 4]
* Meeting minutes, review findings and actions taken to improve the development rules.[cite: 4]
* Version history or change log of secure development procedures showing updates made as a result of reviews.[cite: 4]
  * Specific sections in the documents highlighting what changes were made and the rationale behind them.[cite: 4]
* Reports from internal and external audits that evaluate the process for reviewing secure development rules.[cite: 4]
* Documentation of change requests related to secure development rules, including those arising from review findings.[cite: 4]
* Logs or records tracking the implementation of changes to ensure they are applied throughout the development process.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall take the appropriate measures to establish, document, implement and monitor configurations, including security configurations of hardware, software, services and networks.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Establish documented processes based on best practices and information security standards (52).[cite: 4]
* Maintain and document detailed configuration settings for the following operating procedures (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * processing and handling of information,[cite: 4]
  * backup,[cite: 4]
  * handling errors or other exceptional conditions,[cite: 4]
  * system restart and recovery procedures,[cite: 4]
  * scheduling requirements, including interdependencies with other systems,[cite: 4]
  * cryptographic mechanisms and settings, and[cite: 4]
  * audit trail and system log information.[cite: 4]
* Consider the following security-related parameters for the configuration settings (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * registry settings,[cite: 4]
  * account, file and directory permission settings, and[cite: 4]
  * settings for functions, ports, protocols, services and remote connections.[cite: 4]
* Employ automated mechanisms to centrally manage, apply and verify configuration settings for software and hardware, including mobile devices and the entity’s connected vehicles.[cite: 4]
  * Where appropriate, implement a configuration management database to catalogue and classify all configuration items (CIs), including their security attributes (e.g. patch level, firewall rules and encryption status).[cite: 4]
* Ensure that all network, software and system configurations adhere to established security and operational standards for functions, ports, protocols and services.[cite: 4]
* Monitor and control changes to the configuration settings in accordance with the entity’s policy on the security of network and information systems and topic-specific policies and procedures.[cite: 4]
* Identify software not authorised to run on the information systems.[cite: 4]
* Where appropriate, regularly review and update software configurations.[cite: 4]
* Where appropriate, identify software programs authorised to run on the information system.[cite: 4]
* Employ a deny-all, permit-by-exception policy to allow authorised software to run.[cite: 4]
* Set up procedures for network service usage to restrict access to necessary services or applications only.[cite: 4]
* Manage a secure baseline configuration for development and test environments separately from the operational baseline configuration, where appropriate.[cite: 4]
* Identify, document and approve any deviations from established configuration settings based on defined exceptions on operational requirements.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* System configuration process, based on good practices and standards, in place and maintained.[cite: 4]
* System configuration tables containing configurations of hardware, software, services and networks.[cite: 4]
* Documented secure baseline configuration containing at least (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * essential capabilities of operation;[cite: 4]
  * restricted use of functions;[cite: 4]
  * security by default;[cite: 4]
  * ports, protocols and/or services allowed.[cite: 4]
* Documented and approved exceptions to the configuration baseline containing the alternative measures in place to ensure the confidentiality, availability and integrity of the CI.[cite: 4]
* Documented secure baseline configuration for development and test environments.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of point 6.3.1., the relevant entities shall:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: lay down and ensure security in configurations for their hardware, software, services and networks;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
