parts.prose: lay down and implement processes and tools to enforce the laid down secure configurations for hardware, software, services and networks, for newly installed systems as well as for systems in operation over their lifetime.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Consider hardening guides/best practices and general cybersecurity principles (e.g. least functionality and least privilege) as a basis for deriving the defined security configurations.[cite: 4]
* Establish, document and maintain configuration settings respecting the access control policy.[cite: 4]
* Where applicable, test the configuration before implementation.[cite: 4]
* Employ security safeguards to detect and respond to unauthorised changes to defined configuration settings.[cite: 4]
* Establish a configuration management plan containing:[cite: 4]
  * roles, responsibilities and configuration management processes and procedures;[cite: 4]
  * a process for identifying CIs throughout the system development life cycle; and[cite: 4]
  * a process for managing the configuration of the CIs throughout their life cycle.[cite: 4]
* Protect the configuration management plan from unauthorised disclosure and modification.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Configuration management plan.[cite: 4]
* Comparison of the configuration plan with the access control lists.[cite: 4]
* Mechanisms, for example logical and physical access controls, encryption and audit logs in place.[cite: 4]
* Documented and approved exceptions to the configuration baseline containing the alternative measures in place to ensure the confidentiality, availability and integrity of the CI.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where appropriate, update configurations at planned intervals or when significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks occur.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review and, where appropriate update (53) configurations at least monthly to ensure that patches have been applied, that the backup has been executed according to the plan and that monitoring is in place to identify and alert to fatal server/device/disk errors without delay.[cite: 4]
* Regularly produce, keep and review change logs regarding the security configuration of information systems.[cite: 4]
* Review and update the configurations after major changes (e.g. software updates) and past incidents.[cite: 4]
* Where feasible, obtain baseline configuration files for key systems and devices to compare against current configurations.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Up-to-date configuration management plan, review comments and/or change logs.[cite: 4]
* Documented results of the review activities.[cite: 4]
* Configuration snapshots taken before and after changes or at regular intervals to verify that reviews are conducted and documented.[cite: 4]
* Audit logs from systems and devices that track configuration changes and reviews.[cite: 4]
* Alerts from monitoring systems that notify administrators of unexpected configurations or changes or deviations from the baseline in critical systems.[cite: 4]
* Audit trails and compliance records from internal and external audits.[cite: 4]
* Minutes from team meetings where configuration reviews and changes are discussed and documented.[cite: 4]
* Records of notifications or reminders sent to relevant employees about upcoming configuration reviews.[cite: 4]
* Records from the configuration management tools to ensure they are kept up to date with accurate configuration information.[cite: 4]
* Incident response records that confirm whether the entity takes into account incidents related the configurations.[cite: 4]

groups.title: 6. SECURITY IN NETWORK AND INFORMATION SYSTEMS ACQUISITION, DEVELOPMENT AND MAINTENANCE

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall apply change management procedures to control changes of network and information systems.[cite: 4] Where applicable, the procedures shall be consistent with the relevant entities’ general policies concerning change management.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account industry-recognised and national standards when developing the change management procedures (54).[cite: 4]
* Consider the following elements for the procedures (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * request for change,[cite: 4]
  * risk assessment,[cite: 4]
  * criteria for categorisation and prioritisation of changes:[cite: 4]
    * associated requirements for the type and scope of the tests to be carried out and[cite: 4]
    * the approvals to be obtained;[cite: 4]
  * requirements for performing rollbacks; and[cite: 4]
  * documentation of the changes and approval of changes.[cite: 4]
* The change management procedures may allow different workflows depending on the criticality of the system, the scope of the change and the urgency (e.g. put in place an ‘emergency intervention workflow’).[cite: 4]
* For each change, record the steps of the procedure followed.[cite: 4]
* Review and approve changes following the change management procedures, prior to implementing them.[cite: 4]
* Implement and test change management procedures to make sure that changes to networks and information systems are always done in a predefined way.[cite: 4]
* Where appropriate, establish a change advisory board (CAB) to oversee and approve changes.[cite: 4] The CAB should evaluate change requests based on risk, impact, resource requirements and alignment with business objectives.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented change management procedures for network and information systems that are based on standards or good practices.[cite: 4]
* For each relevant change, a record describing the steps and the result of the change.[cite: 4]
* A system maintenance procedure that addresses:[cite: 4]
  * roles;[cite: 4]
  * purpose;[cite: 4]
  * scope;[cite: 4]
  * responsibilities;[cite: 4]
  * management commitment, if applicable;[cite: 4]
  * coordination among different organisational units; and[cite: 4]
  * compliance.[cite: 4]
* Logs that record the dates and outcomes of the periodic reviews of the change, repair and maintenance procedures.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The procedures referred to in point 6.4.1. shall be applied for releases, modifications and emergency changes of any software and hardware in operation and changes to the configuration.[cite: 4] The procedures shall ensure that those changes are documented and, based on the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1, tested and assessed in view of the potential impact before being implemented.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Consider a mandatory integrity check before installing and deploying new software.[cite: 4]
* Ensure, where appropriate, that changes are done in an authenticated, authorised and non-repudiating manner.[cite: 4]
* Test and validate changes before they are implemented in operational systems, where applicable.[cite: 4] Where appropriate, a security impact analysis may be performed in a separate test environment before implementation in an operational environment.[cite: 4]
* Take all necessary precautions before making changes (back up images, for instance).[cite: 4]
* Schedule, perform, document and review records of maintenance and repairs on system components in accordance with the supplier’s specifications and/or the entity’s requirements.[cite: 4]
* Ensure that changes are only allowed with approved tools and that their execution is documented.[cite: 4]
* Restrict the use of maintenance tools to authorised personnel only.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Logs and records of past (new) software installations.[cite: 4]
* Evidence that MFA is in place for activating change, repair and maintenance procedures, where applicable.[cite: 4]
* Test plans and results that demonstrate the implementation and effectiveness of the change, repair and maintenance procedures.[cite: 4]
* If the entity utilises change management tools, evidence that these tools enforce the use of approved resources only and mandate documentation for each change.[cite: 4]
* Access control lists (ACLs) to verify that access to the tools is in line with the access control policy.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: In the event that the regular change management procedures could not be followed due to an emergency, the relevant entities shall document the result of the change and the explanation for why the procedures could not be followed.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Where appropriate, integrate the pullback scenario (55) into the change management procedures.[cite: 4]
* Assess the risks from legacy systems and upgrade existing legacy systems to include security mitigating measures in case appropriate security cannot be achieved.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that regular change control procedures that could not be followed due to an emergency change are applied immediately after the emergency change.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documentation with specific pullback plans.[cite: 4]
* Logs and records from past change requests with details of (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * the change,[cite: 4]
  * reason for emergency,[cite: 4]
  * approval,[cite: 4]
  * reason for delay,[cite: 4]
  * follow up actions and[cite: 4]
  * how to revert the system to a previous stage if the change fails.[cite: 4]
* Logs and records from past legacy system upgrade that contain risk assessments and the reasoning for the change.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where appropriate, update the procedures at planned intervals and when significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review the change management procedures at least once every two years.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that the management procedures cover planned and unplanned changes and the development phase, when applicable.[cite: 4]
* Ensure that the process is not bypassed.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Review plans or schedules.[cite: 4]
* Up to date change management procedures, review comments and/or change logs.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of approval and monitoring of maintenance activities, whether performed on site or remotely and whether the equipment is serviced on site or removed to another location.[cite: 4]
* Logs of all changes made to the procedures, including details, approvals and implementation dates.[cite: 4]
* Audit trails and compliance records from internal and external audits.[cite: 4]
* Logs of significant incidents to confirm whether they include documentation of reviews and updates to the change, repair and maintenance procedures.[cite: 4]
* Reports from post-incident reviews that document any necessary adjustments to the procedures following significant incidents.[cite: 4]
* Records showing how changes and updates to the procedures were implemented and reviewed.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall establish, implement and apply a policy and procedures for security testing.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account industry-recognised standards when developing the testing policy (56).[cite: 4]
* Establish and maintain a testing programme appropriate to the entity’s size, complexity and maturity (57).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented security testing and procedures based on relevant standards and good practices.[cite: 4]
* Guidelines and standards that the entity adheres to for conducting security tests.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: establish, based on the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1, the need, scope, frequency and type of security tests;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: carry out security tests according to a documented test methodology, covering the components identified as relevant for secure operation in a risk analysis;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: document the type, scope, time and results of the tests, including assessment of criticality and mitigating actions for each finding;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: apply mitigating actions in case of critical findings.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Make sure that network and information systems undergo continuous testing, particularly in environments utilizing continuous integration / continuous deployment practices.[cite: 4] Regular testing should be conducted at set-up, after significant upgrades or modifications and following maintenance, to maintain robust security and performance.[cite: 4]
* Consider a range of security tests (e.g. vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, code review, ethical hacking, bug bounty programmes, cyber attack simulations, red teaming, protocol conformance testing or cyber response exercises) and select the most appropriate one (or more) to test the specific procedure, service or tool over time.[cite: 4]
* Entity-wide scoped tests should be carried out at planned intervals or when significant incidents or changes occur.[cite: 4]
* Conduct internal and/or external audits throughout the entity’s networks, systems and processes in an ad-hoc manner.[cite: 4]
* Record evidence while testing.[cite: 4] The need, scope, frequency, type and results are to be documented in a manner that is comprehensible to an expert third party.[cite: 4]
* Use criteria to assess the results of the tests similar to the criteria for performing cybersecurity risk assessments (guidance on point 2.1.2 of the Annex to the regulation).[cite: 4]
* Assess, follow up and remediate high-criticality findings with respect to the confidentiality, integrity, authenticity or availability of the service provided.[cite: 4]
* Document the assessment of criticality and mitigating actions for each finding.[cite: 4] Ensure that risk assessment results and risk treatment plans are updated accordingly (Annex to the regulation, point 2.1).[cite: 4]
* When testing reveals an underlying security issue in a free and open source component, these findings must be shared with the relevant open source project.[cite: 4] If a patch is developed to address the issue, the relevant code should also be shared with the relevant open source project, in a manner suitable for integration.[cite: 4]
* Where appropriate, any automated security tests written by entities for open source components that they use, should be shared with the relevant open source projects.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented security testing policy and procedures that include the elements referred to in point 5.2 (a) of the Annex to the regulation.[cite: 4]
* Documentation defining the roles and responsibilities of personnel involved in security testing.[cite: 4]
* Plans or schedules for upcoming or completed regular or ad hoc tests.[cite: 4]
* List of reports from past security tests.[cite: 4] This should cover various types of testing (e.g. vulnerability assessments, penetration testing and code reviews).[cite: 4]
* Internal or external audit reports.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where appropriate, update their security testing policies at planned intervals.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review the security testing policy and procedures at least once every two years.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Updated security-testing policy and procedures, review comments, and/or change logs.[cite: 4]
* Security-testing policy and procedures, including when tests must be carried out, test plans, test cases and test report templates.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall specify and apply procedures, coherent with the change management procedures referred to in point 6.4.1. as well as with vulnerability management, risk management and other relevant management procedures, for ensuring that:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: security patches are applied within a reasonable time after they become available;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: security patches are tested before being applied in production systems;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: security patches come from trusted sources and are checked for integrity;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: additional measures are implemented and residual risks are accepted in cases where a patch is not available or not applied pursuant to point 6.6.2.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account well known standards when developing the security patch management procedures (58).[cite: 4]
* Actions may vary, depending on the network and information system (e.g. mandatory patching for all exposed systems or internet-connected devices such as firewalls or routers, and limited patching only in specific circumstances, for instance in isolated or legacy systems where regular patching may not be feasible or available).[cite: 4]
* Establish a process, in combination with the asset inventory, for being informed when a new security patch is published and schedule patch roll-outs accordingly.[cite: 4]
* Patching should be a standard activity in normal maintenance and outage planning of services.[cite: 4] Nonetheless, some failures may require immediate patching depending on their criticality.[cite: 4]
* Prioritise and apply patches based on risk.[cite: 4] Evaluate the severity of the vulnerability, exposure of the affected system and likelihood of exploitation.[cite: 4]
* Deploy vulnerability management technologies to identify unpatched and misconfigured software.[cite: 4]
* Define your relevant security information sources considering your assets and continuously monitor them for patch announcements, patch and non-patch remediation, and general threats.[cite: 4]
* Verify the patch sources through (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * digital certificates to verify the vendor;[cite: 4]
  * digital signatures of the patches[cite: 4]
  * change logs provided by the vendor; and[cite: 4]
  * feedback from the community concerning the reliability of the vendor.[cite: 4]
* Consider a strategy for applying patches after approval or testing following the change management procedure (indicative, non exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * Blue/green allows the patches to be applied first in an isolated environment identical to the production environment, and then in the production environment.[cite: 4] This ensures zero downtime and an immediate rollback option.[cite: 4]
  * Rolling (59) deployment allows gradual updates of parts of the production environment, one set of servers or instances at a time, rather than deploying a patch all at once.[cite: 4] It is ideal for large and distributed environments.[cite: 4]
  * Feature toggles allow new features or patches to be deployed to production but keep them disabled until they are ready to be used.[cite: 4] They are suitable for control over new features or patches when they are turned on, making it easy to test and release.[cite: 4]
  * Shadow deployment allows new code or patches to be deployed directly to production but it shadows live traffic by mirroring user requests to both the current and new systems to observe how the new version behaves without affecting the user experience.[cite: 4] It is ideal for testing new features in production without affecting users.[cite: 4]
  * Hotfix deployments are used for critical patches that need to be applied immediately to address severe issues.[cite: 4]
* Where appropriate and to reduce risks related to significant updates in important dependencies, consider performing a trial using release candidates (60) of these components, to get an early indication of incompatibilities or breaking changes, so they may be remedied.[cite: 4] If any of these components are open source software, offer feedback about any issues found during this trial.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Detailed procedures and guidelines for how patches are identified, evaluated, tested, deployed and verified.[cite: 4]
* Logs or records showing the history of patch deployments across various systems.[cite: 4] These may include (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * timestamps;[cite: 4]
  * responsible personnel; and[cite: 4]
  * affected systems.[cite: 4]
* Evidence that the asset inventory (Annex to the regulation, point 12.4) is updated after a new security patch is announced, if possible accompanied by the time plan for applying it.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of testing patches before deployment in a controlled environment.[cite: 4] This should include results of testing and any issues encountered and resolved.[cite: 4]
* Documentation of test plans and results for patches before deployment to production environments.[cite: 4]
* Documentation of change requests for deploying patches, including approvals and impact assessments.[cite: 4]
* Detailed audit trails showing the steps taken from patch identification to deployment.[cite: 4]
* Checks for the latest patches.[cite: 4]
* Approved documented actions for applying patches.[cite: 4]
* Records of changes logged, reviewed and approved.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of vendor verification mechanisms for example digital certificates and digital signatures.[cite: 4]
* Reports from internal and external audits evaluating the effectiveness of the patch management processes.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: By way of derogation from point 6.6.1.(a), the relevant entities may choose not to apply security patches when the disadvantages of applying the security patches outweigh the cybersecurity benefits.[cite: 4] The relevant entities shall duly document and substantiate the reasons for any such decision.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Make an effort, proportionate to the entity’s size and importance, to ensure that security patches do not introduce additional vulnerabilities or instabilities.[cite: 4] Examples of information supporting such a decision may include (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * vendor documentation on the patch:[cite: 4]
    * what specific vulnerabilities or bugs are addressed,[cite: 4]
    * whether the patch fixes a security issue, improves performance, adds features or resolves stability concerns,[cite: 4]
    * system requirements or any specific configurations required or changes to system settings,[cite: 4]
    * installation instructions on How to apply the patch and whether it requires a restart or additional configuration;[cite: 4]
  * severity rating - patches that address critical vulnerabilities are more likely to apply; and[cite: 4]
  * security blogs, forums and mailing lists for any known issues or incompatibilities introduced by the patch.[cite: 4]
* If patching is not feasible, consider alternative measures such as strict configuration hardening, intrusion detection systems, regular vulnerability scanning, network segmentation or isolation where feasible, access control and monitoring.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Evidence of patch prioritisation for example emphasis is placed on patches assessed as critical.[cite: 4]
* Evidence that residual risks resulting from non-patching are listed and mitigated.[cite: 4]
* Incident reports related to unpatched vulnerabilities to check the effectiveness of the mitigation measures during the entity’s response.[cite: 4]
* Logs of changes made to systems, including patches applied, rollback procedures and any issues encountered.[cite: 4]
* Documented decisions no to patch accompanied by relevant alternative measures.[cite: 4]
* Up-to-date risk-treatment plan.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall take the appropriate measures to protect their network and information systems from cyber threats.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account well known standards when implementing measures for network security (61).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented network security measures that are based on relevant standards and good practices.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of point 6.7.1., the relevant entities shall:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: document the architecture of the network in a comprehensible and up to date manner;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: determine and apply controls to protect the relevant entities’ internal network domains from unauthorised access;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: configure controls to prevent accesses and network communication not required for the operation of the relevant entities;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: determine and apply controls for remote access to network and information systems, including access by service providers;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: not use systems used for administration of the security policy implementation for other purposes;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: explicitly forbid or deactivate unneeded connections and services;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: where appropriate, exclusively allow access to the relevant entities’ network and information systems by devices authorised by those entities;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: allow connections of service providers only after an authorisation request and for a set time period, such as the duration of a maintenance operation;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: establish communication between distinct systems only through trusted channels that are isolated using logical, cryptographic or physical separation from other communication channels and provide assured identification of their end points and protection of the channel data from modification or disclosure;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: adopt an implementation plan for the full transition towards latest generation network layer communication protocols in a secure, appropriate and gradual way and establish measures to accelerate such transition;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: adopt an implementation plan for the deployment of internationally agreed and interoperable modern e-mail communications standards to secure e-mail communications to mitigate vulnerabilities linked to e-mail-related threats and establish measures to accelerate such deployment;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: apply best practices for the security of the DNS and for Internet routing security and routing hygiene of traffic originating from and destined to the network.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Implement secure-by-design principles by integrating security at every layer of network design including the physical, data link, network, transport and application layers.[cite: 4]
* Implement secure configurations for wireless networks.[cite: 4]
* Where appropriate, consider zero-trust (62) network access.[cite: 4]
* Identify the technical measures for the transition to the latest network layer communication protocols (e.g. transition to Internet Protocol version 6).[cite: 4]
* Define roles, responsibilities and timelines for the transition to latest-generation network layer communication protocols.[cite: 4]
* Approve, log and perform remote maintenance of network and information systems in a manner that prevents unauthorised access.[cite: 4]
* Consider the following for email communications (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * standards such as Start transport layer security (STARTTLS), DNS-based authentication of named entities (DANE), domain-based message authentication, reporting and& conformance (DMARC), DomainKeys identified mail (DKIM) and sender policy framework (63),[cite: 4]
  * internal spam/scam/virus filtering and[cite: 4]
  * URL rewriting, URL scanning and URL detonation in a sandbox.[cite: 4]
* Consider DNS security good practices (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * deploying DNS security extensions (DNS SEC) (64),[cite: 4]
  * deploying protective DNS, wherever technically feasible, to provide additional network-wide security capabilities,[cite: 4]
  * encrypting DNS traffic, both internal and external, wherever feasible,[cite: 4]
  * deploying dedicated DNS servers to reduce attack surface and[cite: 4]
  * following all technical guidance on ensuring that DNS deployments and the DNS protocol are as secure and resilient as possible.[cite: 4]
* Consider Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) (65) for internet routing.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Up-to-date network diagrams, including OOB connections.[cite: 4]
* Firewall(s) configured in accordance with the network traffic rules of the entity’s policies.[cite: 4]
* Configuration files and rulesets for firewalls and routers, showing how traffic is filtered and managed.[cite: 4]
* Secure configurations for wireless networks for example use of WPA3 (encryption), 802.1X with EAP (authentication), firmware updates.[cite: 4]
* Configuration files for switches, including virtual local access network (VLAN) settings and ACLs.[cite: 4]
* Documentation of ACLs implemented on network devices to control traffic flow.[cite: 4]
* Documented correct usage of mobile devices, including the entity’s connected vehicles that can store data locally on the vehicle and/or share data externally by means of telematics and other remote accesses (e.g. teleworking and OOB connections).[cite: 4]
* Evidence of controls over privileged accounts, including logs and policies.[cite: 4]
* A list of all devices used (network components), if any, that cannot receive security patches and are not up to date.[cite: 4]
* Access logs to confirm that only authorised personnel make changes and conduct reviews of the network security rules.[cite: 4]
* Transition to the latest generation plan for implementing network layer communication protocols.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where appropriate, update these measures at planned intervals and when significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks occur.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Although the frequency of reviews of network security measures depends on the entity’s risk assessment as a general rule the entity might (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * continuously monitor the networks for real time threats;[cite: 4]
  * perform scans for new vulnerabilities weekly;[cite: 4]
  * review and possibly update the rules of the firewall and other tools monthly; and[cite: 4]
  * thoroughly assess the entire network annually.[cite: 4]
* Review logs or records of all changes made to the network security rules, including details of the changes, approvals and implementation dates.[cite: 4]
* Ensure that these reviews are conducted regularly and documented comprehensively.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Plans or schedules for upcoming or completed, regular or ad hoc reviews.[cite: 4]
* List of reports from past reviews.[cite: 4] This should cover various types of reviews.[cite: 4]
* Logs from firewalls, routers and other network devices showing access attempts, configuration changes and other relevant activities.[cite: 4]
* Reports from SIEM and EDR/XDR systems showing aggregated and analysed security events.[cite: 4]
* Virtual private network (VPN) and remote access logs showing remote access, including OOB connections, access attempts, successful connections and any anomalies.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of network access control (NAC) or other similar and/or alternative solutions, in place, including logs and configuration settings.[cite: 4]
* Logs or records showing the dates and results of regular reviews of the network security rules.[cite: 4]
* Logs or records of all changes made to the network security rules.[cite: 4]
* Logs or records of firewall and ACL reviews.[cite: 4]
* Documentation showing regular reviews of user and administrative access to network devices.[cite: 4]
* Audit logs from network security devices (e.g. firewalls, intrusion detection/prevention systems (IDS/IPS)) to ensure that changes and reviews are logged.[cite: 4]
* Backup files of network device configurations to ensure that changes and reviews are reflected in the backups.[cite: 4]
* Logs of network security incidents to see if they include documentation of rule set reviews following significant incidents.[cite: 4]
* Post incident review reports to see if they document reviews and any necessary adjustments to the network security rules.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall segment systems into networks or zones in accordance with the results of the risk assessment referred to in point 2.1.[cite: 4] They shall segment their systems and networks from third parties’ systems and networks.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account well known standards when segmenting networks (66).[cite: 4]
* Integrate the segmentation derived from the risk assessment into the network diagram.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented network segmentation rules based on relevant standards and good practices.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For that purpose, the relevant entities shall:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: consider the functional, logical and physical relationship, including location, between trustworthy systems and services;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: grant access to a network or zone based on an assessment of its security requirements;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: keep systems that are critical to the relevant entities operation or to safety in secured zones;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: deploy a demilitarised zone within their communication networks to ensure secure communication originating from or destined to their networks;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: restrict access and communications between and within zones to those necessary for the operation of the relevant entities or for safety;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: separate the dedicated network for administration of network and information systems from the relevant entities’ operational network;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: segregate network administration channels from other network traffic;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: separate the production systems for the relevant entities’ services from systems used in development and testing, including backups.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Make sure that the segments are in line with the results of the risk assessment (Annex to the regulation, point 2.1).[cite: 4]
* Apply a graduated set of measures in different logical network domains to further segregate the network security environments, including:[cite: 4]
  * internal networks;[cite: 4]
  * publicly accessible systems;[cite: 4]
  * OOB connections; and[cite: 4]
  * assets with high criticality.[cite: 4]
* Implement subnetworks for publicly accessible system components that are physically and/or logically separate from internal organisational networks.[cite: 4]
* Determine the degree of physical separation of system components from physically distinct components:[cite: 4]
  * in separate racks in the same room,[cite: 4]
  * in separate rooms for the components with high criticality and[cite: 4]
  * more significant geographical separation of the components with high criticality.[cite: 4]
* Implement separate network addresses (that is, different subnets) to connect to systems in different security domains.[cite: 4]
* Monitor and control communications at the external boundary of the system as well as at key internal boundaries within the system, including segmentation violations.[cite: 4]
* Where appropriate, isolate information security tools, mechanisms and support components from other internal information system components, where appropriate (69), by implementing physically separate subnetworks with managed interfaces to other components of the system.[cite: 4]
* Route all networked, privileged accesses through a dedicated, managed interface for the purposes of access control and auditing.[cite: 4]
* Implement a managed interface for each external telecommunication service.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Risk assessments that justify the segmentation decisions.[cite: 4]
* Interviews with IT and security staff to understand the rationale behind network segmentation.[cite: 4]
* Up-to-date network diagrams showing segmentation into different networks or zones (e.g. DMZ (70), internal networks and guest networks).[cite: 4]
* Verification that the diagrams align with business functions and risk profiles.[cite: 4]
* Documented criteria for creating and maintaining different network zones.[cite: 4]
* VLAN configurations on network switches and routers.[cite: 4]
* VLANs corresponding to different security zones and business functions.[cite: 4]
* Measures (e.g. IDS/IPS and monitoring systems) tailored to each network zone.[cite: 4]
* Configurations of network devices (e.g. routers, switches and firewalls) for appropriate segmentation settings.[cite: 4]
* Configuration settings that match documented segmentation rules and diagrams.[cite: 4]
* ACLs that consider segregation of duties.[cite: 4]
* Firewall configurations.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where appropriate, update network segmentation at planned intervals and when significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review and, if necessary, update the process for network segmentation rules at least annually.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Reports from recent penetration tests and/or vulnerability scans.[cite: 4]
* Plans or schedules for reviewing network segmentation rules.[cite: 4]
* Logs or records confirming that the reviews have been conducted in accordance with the schedule.[cite: 4]
* Change management documentation for network segmentation changes, in line with risk-assessment results and business needs.[cite: 4]
* Incident response documentation to verify that network segmentation rules are reviewed following significant security incidents.[cite: 4]
* Post-incident analysis reports that include assessments of segmentation rule effectiveness and any necessary adjustments.[cite: 4]
* Internal or external audit logs and reports that cover network segmentation rule reviews.[cite: 4]
* Reviews performed periodically and in response to network changes or incidents.[cite: 4]
* Minutes from security or IT operations meetings where network segmentation rules are discussed.[cite: 4]
* Penetration tests and vulnerability assessments that include evaluations of network segmentation.[cite: 4]
* Tests conducted periodically and after major changes or incidents and findings leading to rule reviews.[cite: 4]

groups.title: 6.9 PROTECTION AGAINST MALICIOUS AND UNAUTHORISED SOFTWARE

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall protect their network and information systems against malicious and unauthorised software.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For that purpose, the relevant entities shall in particular implement measures that detect or prevent the use of malicious or unauthorised software.[cite: 4] The relevant entities shall, where appropriate, ensure that their network and information systems are equipped with detection and response software, which is updated regularly in accordance with the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1 and the contractual agreements with the providers.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Employ mechanisms for detecting and protecting against malicious and unauthorised software at system entry and exit points and at workstations, servers and mobile computing devices on the network to detect and eradicate malicious code transported by electronic mail, electronic mail attachments, web accesses or removable media or inserted through the exploitation of system vulnerabilities.[cite: 4]
* Configure malicious code protection mechanisms to:[cite: 4]
  * be active all the time;[cite: 4]
  * perform periodic scans of the system regularly and real-time scans of files from external sources as the files are downloaded, opened or executed;[cite: 4]
  * generate notifications when suspected malicious and unauthorised software is detected;[cite: 4]
  * disinfect and quarantine infected files; and[cite: 4]
  * restore system settings and ensure that critical settings cannot be disabled or restricted.[cite: 4]
* Apply application whitelisting and monitor unauthorised activities and system behaviour, where appropriate.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that the malicious and unauthorised protection mechanisms are centrally managed, where appropriate.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that there are mechanisms that prevent users from circumventing malicious and unauthorised software protection capabilities.[cite: 4]
* Make sure that spam protection mechanisms are employed at system entry points such as workstations, servers or mobile computing devices on the network.[cite: 4]
* Update malicious code protection mechanisms (including signature definitions) whenever new releases are available in accordance with configuration rules and the entity’s patch management procedures.[cite: 4]
* Address issues related to false positives during malicious code detection and eradication and the resulting potential impact on system availability.[cite: 4]
* Align rules for monitoring and logging malicious and unauthorised detection and repair software with the entity’s monitoring and logging tools and procedures (Annex to the regulation, point 3.2) and with the entity’s access control (Annex to the regulation, point 11.1) and asset-handling policy.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Endpoint protection systems (EPS), such as endpoint protection platform (EPP) and endpoint detection and response (EDR), across the network.[cite: 4]
* Malware detection system present and up to date.[cite: 4]
* Tools for monitoring unauthorised software is in place and up to date.[cite: 4]
* Firewall configurations, IDS/IPS and secure web gateways containing malicious and unauthorised software protection measures.[cite: 4]
* Use of whitelisting solutions, which restrict the execution of non-approved software and code.[cite: 4]
* Rules and configurations related to application whitelisting up to date.[cite: 4]
* Documented description of centrally managed tools.[cite: 4]
* Records of recent updates of mechanisms for detecting and protecting against malicious/unauthorised software showing that they are regularly patched and updated to protect against known vulnerabilities.[cite: 4]
* Records of periodic scans.[cite: 4]
* Monitoring and logging of network and information systems, at intervals to identify malicious code and unauthorized code execution.[cite: 4]
* Logs of blocked or detected threats.[cite: 4]
* Logs recorded and maintained covering:[cite: 4]
  * user activities;[cite: 4]
  * exceptions; and[cite: 4]
  * information security incidents.[cite: 4]
* Documented spam protection mechanism.[cite: 4]
* Risk assessment to determine the level of logs monitoring required.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall obtain information about technical vulnerabilities in their network and information systems, evaluate their exposure to such vulnerabilities and take appropriate measures to manage the vulnerabilities.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Adopt a framework for assessing the severity of vulnerabilities based on models (e.g. CVSS, exploit prediction scoring system (EPSS) or SANS vulnerability assessment framework) and supplemented by environmental and threat metrics as appropriate.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documentation of a risk-assessment framework used to evaluate the severity, impact and probability of exploitation of identified vulnerabilities (e.g. CVSS scores).[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of point 6.10.1., the relevant entities shall:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: monitor information about vulnerabilities through appropriate channels, such as announcements of CSIRTs, competent authorities or information provided by suppliers or service providers;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: perform, where appropriate, vulnerability scans and record evidence of the results of the scans, at planned intervals;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: address, without undue delay, vulnerabilities identified by the relevant entities as critical to their operations;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: ensure that their vulnerability handling is compatible with their change management, security patch management, risk management and incident management procedures;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: lay down a procedure for disclosing vulnerabilities in accordance with the applicable national coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* As a minimum, address vulnerabilities assigned to higher classifications (e.g. ‘critical’ and ‘high’ in the CVSS) or equivalent (e.g. as defined by the national CSIRT) without undue delay.[cite: 4] Where possible, accepting the risk of such vulnerabilities and not addressing them is not advisable.[cite: 4]
* Share information obtained from technical vulnerability scans with designated personnel throughout the entity and with authorities to help eliminate similar vulnerabilities in other information systems.[cite: 4]
* Disclose as yet unknown vulnerabilities to designated CSIRTs in accordance with national coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) policies, where applicable.[cite: 4]
* Identify a single point of contact and channels for communication with suppliers and service providers about issues related to network and information security.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Logs of a vulnerability assessed as critical to check if it was addressed.[cite: 4]
* Licences or subscriptions for vulnerability-scanning tools.[cite: 4]
* Configuration files of the vulnerability-scanning tools to ensure they are set up to scan the entire relevant infrastructure and are updated with the latest vulnerability definitions.[cite: 4]
* Logs from vulnerability management tools showing scan schedules, results and follow-up actions.[cite: 4]
* Documented technical vulnerability scan reports.[cite: 4]
* SIEM and EDR/XDR logs for records of detected vulnerabilities and related alerts from monitoring channels.[cite: 4]
* Reports from third-party security assessments or penetration tests.[cite: 4]
* For vulnerabilities assessed as critical, evidence that findings from these assessments have been addressed.[cite: 4]
* Records of any vulnerabilities disclosed, in accordance with the national CVD policy.[cite: 4]
* Interview with the single point of contact and channels for communication with suppliers and service providers about information-security-related issues.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: When justified by the potential impact of the vulnerability, the relevant entities shall create and implement a plan to mitigate the vulnerability.[cite: 4] In other cases, the relevant entities shall document and substantiate the reason why the vulnerability does not require remediation.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Ensure comprehensive documentation of identified vulnerabilities, the associated risk assessments and any mitigation plans developed.[cite: 4]
* Define and establish the roles and responsibilities associated with vulnerability management.[cite: 4]
* Mitigation plans should include clear timelines, assigned responsibilities and follow-up procedures.[cite: 4]
* All mitigation plans, along with the rationale for non-remediation decisions, should be reviewed and validated by the management body responsible for risk oversight.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Records showing timelines and responsible employees for each remediation effort and verification of fixes.[cite: 4]
* Records or logs of past vulnerability mitigation plans or schedules.[cite: 4]
* Records of any vulnerability that was not addressed and the justification for not addressing it.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where appropriate, update at planned intervals the channels they use for monitoring vulnerability information.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review the information from the technical-vulnerability-monitoring channels at least biannually.[cite: 4]
* Consider inventorying sources likely to report technical vulnerabilities in the identified components and distribute updates (software publisher websites, CERT website and ENISA website) (71).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* List of monitoring channels for technical vulnerabilities, including suppliers and service providers’ single points of contact.[cite: 4]
* Records of past reviews and plans for future reviews of technical vulnerability channels.[cite: 4]
* Subscriptions to relevant vulnerability notification services, mailing lists and alert systems (e.g. CERT, vendor advisories and security forums).[cite: 4]
* Logs that document periodic reviews of the monitoring channels to verify that they are up to date and effective.[cite: 4]
* Records of alerts or notifications received from monitoring channels about new vulnerabilities, including how these alerts were handled and any subsequent actions taken.[cite: 4]
* Logs that record the monitoring activities for vulnerability information, including dates and sources monitored (e.g. security advisories, vendor bulletins, threat intelligence feeds).[cite: 4]

groups.title: 7. POLICIES AND PROCEDURES TO ASSESS THE EFFECTIVENESS OF CYBERSECURITY RISK-MANAGEMENT MEASURES

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of Article 21(2), point (f) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the relevant entities shall establish, implement and apply a policy and procedures to assess whether the cybersecurity risk-management measures taken by the relevant entity are effectively implemented and maintained.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Take into account industry-recognised standards when developing the policy and procedures for assessing the efficient implementation of the measures (72).[cite: 4]
* Implement a policy for assessing the effectiveness of implementation of measures that is proportionate to the risk posture of the entity in line with the risk assessment.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented policy and procedures for effectiveness assessments based on good practices and standards (73).[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy and procedures referred to in point 7.1. shall take into account results of the risk assessment pursuant to point 2.1. and past significant incidents.[cite: 4] The relevant entities shall determine:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: what cybersecurity risk-management measures are to be monitored and measured, including processes and controls;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the methods for monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation, as applicable, to ensure valid results;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: when the monitoring and measuring is to be performed;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: who is responsible for monitoring and measuring the effectiveness of the cybersecurity risk-management measures;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: when the results from monitoring and measurement are to be analysed and evaluated;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: who has to analyse and evaluate these results.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* When selecting measures for assessing effectiveness of implementation take into account the cost of their implementation.[cite: 4]
* Consider one or more of the following indicative methods for assessing the effectiveness of implementation of a measure, according to the risk-treatment plan (section 2.1):[cite: 4]
  * self-assessment,[cite: 4]
  * benchmarking against a measure’s checklist or a standard,[cite: 4]
  * vulnerability assessment,[cite: 4]
  * penetration testing (e.g. internal, external, red/blue team),[cite: 4]
  * secure code review,[cite: 4]
  * audit (e.g. internal, external, compliance) and[cite: 4]
  * performance monitoring.[cite: 4]
* The assessment service can be provided by an external entity or by specially authorised employees of the entity.[cite: 4]
  * In the case of external entities, confidentiality and non-disclosure terms should be included in the contract.[cite: 4]
  * Internal employees should be suitably trained, based on the skills required for the objective of their role and the entity should consider their objectivity and impartiality, where possible.[cite: 4] The entity should pay particular attention to the elements of point 2.3. of the Annex to the regulation concerning the impartiality of the employees.[cite: 4] For instance, employees should not come from the department or division whose systems are being inspected and should not have been involved in developing the code or in installing or operating the system being audited for this purpose.[cite: 4]
* Define key performance indicators (KPIs) to measure the effectiveness of measures including, one or more, notable examples such as (indicative, non-exhaustive list) (74):[cite: 4]
  * the cost of implementation and maintenance, for example capital expenditure (CAPEX) / operational expenditure (OPEX);[cite: 4]
  * the number of employees who have attended cybersecurity trainings (75);[cite: 4]
  * the number of vulnerabilities detected;[cite: 4]
  * time to remediation;[cite: 4]
  * the number of incidents;[cite: 4]
  * the number of incidents related to a change;[cite: 4]
  * incident response times; and[cite: 4]
  * number of non-compliances (consider the elements in point 2.2 of the Annex to the regulation concerning compliance monitoring).[cite: 4]
* If possible, use the same KPIs for each assessment and utilize standardized templates and checklists to ensure consistency and thoroughness.[cite: 4]
* Although the frequency of monitoring and measurement of measures, addressed in point 7.2.1 (a) of the Annex to the regulation, depends on the entity's risk assessment, the entity may follow this indicative, non-exhaustive guideline:[cite: 4]
  * continuously monitor and measure the effectiveness of mitigating measures designed to address real-time threats (e.g. firewalls, IDS/IPS);[cite: 4]
  * monitor and measure the effectiveness of security measures related to the threat landscape biannually (e.g. vulnerability management and incident response plans);[cite: 4]
  * assess the overall effectiveness of all measures annually;[cite: 4]
  * assess the effectiveness of measures related to a specific incident following that incident; and[cite: 4]
  * assess the effectiveness of measures related to a specific system or one of its components following significant changes to this system or this component.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Evidence that management has received reporting on the effective implementation of the measures.[cite: 4]
* Evidence that monitoring and measurement results are reported to the management bodies (Annex to the regulation, point 2.3.3 concerning compliance monitoring).[cite: 4]
* Documented objectives and KPIs for the implementation of the measures.[cite: 4]
* Documented analysis and evaluation of the results from previous evaluations.[cite: 4]
* Logs or records from previous effectiveness assessments.[cite: 4]
* Plans or schedules for future effectiveness assessments.[cite: 4]
* Documented roles and responsibilities.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where appropriate, update the policy and procedures at planned intervals and when significant incidents or significant changes to operations or risks.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Review policy and procedures for the assessment of the effectiveness of the measures at least every two years, taking into account:[cite: 4]
  * changes to the information systems;[cite: 4]
  * changes to the environment of operation; and[cite: 4]
  * trends related to threats and vulnerabilities (take into account root cause analysis) (76).[cite: 4]
* Update the policy and procedures based on findings from security tests (Annex to the regulation, point 6.5.2 (c)) and the independent review of the policy on the security of the network and information systems (Annex to the regulation, point 2.3.3), if applicable.[cite: 4]
* Take into account the results of the assessment and consider them when identifying and prioritising appropriate risk-treatment options and measures (Annex to the regulation, point 2.1.3).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Logs or records from previous policy reviews.[cite: 4]
* Plans or schedules for future effectiveness assessment reviews.[cite: 4]
* Risk-treatment plan that takes into account the results of the effectiveness assessments.[cite: 4]
* Minutes from meetings where security-testing results are discussed and the effectiveness of other policies is reviewed and improvements to them are discussed based on these results.[cite: 4]
* Records showing updates to other policies and procedures with a view to assessing their effectiveness.[cite: 4]

groups.title: 8. BASIC CYBER HYGIENE PRACTICES AND SECURITY TRAINING
8.1 AWARENESS RAISING AND BASIC CYBER HYGIENE PRACTICES

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of Article 21(2), point (g) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the relevant entities shall ensure that their employees are aware of risks, are informed of the importance of cybersecurity and apply cyber hygiene practices.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Implement cybersecurity awareness programmes:[cite: 4]
  * use various formats, such as workshops, webinars and e-learning modules;[cite: 4]
  * use multiple communication channels (emails, newsletters and intranet) to keep employees informed about cybersecurity updates, risks and cyber hygiene practices for users.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Awareness raising programme, for example a comprehensive outline of the programme, detailing its objectives, content, frequency, syllabus and schedule.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of point 8.1.1., the relevant entities shall offer to all employees, including members of management bodies, as well as to direct suppliers and service providers where appropriate in accordance with point 5.1.4, an awareness raising programme, which shall:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: be scheduled over time, so that the activities are repeated and cover new employees;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: be established in line with the network and information security policy, topic-specific policies and relevant procedures on network and information security;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: cover cybersecurity risk-management measures in place, contact points and resources for additional information and advice on cybersecurity matters, as well as cyber hygiene practices for users.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Include cyber hygiene practices (77) for relevant users (indicative, non-exhaustive list):[cite: 4]
  * clear desk and screen policy,[cite: 4]
  * use of relevant strong authentication means and methods, multi factor passwords etc,[cite: 4]
  * event reporting,[cite: 4]
  * safe email use and web browsing,[cite: 4]
  * protection from phishing and social engineering,[cite: 4]
  * secure use of mobile devices,[cite: 4]
  * secure use of the entity’s connected-vehicles,[cite: 4]
  * secure connection practices,[cite: 4]
  * backup practices,[cite: 4]
  * zero-trust concept,[cite: 4]
  * software updates,[cite: 4]
  * secure device configuration,[cite: 4]
  * network segmentation,[cite: 4]
  * secure teleworking practices.[cite: 4]
* Include the following in the programme (indicative, non-exhaustive list).[cite: 4]
  * Train personnel on the policy on the security of network and information systems.[cite: 4]
  * Train personnel to recognize social engineering attacks, such as phishing, pre-texting and tailgating.[cite: 4]
  * Train personnel to be aware of causes of unintentional data exposure.[cite: 4] Example topics include the erroneous delivery of sensitive data, losing a portable end-user device, providing unauthorized access to an entity’s connected-vehicle and the data stored on it and publishing data to unintended audiences.[cite: 4]
  * Train personnel on the dangers of connecting to and transmitting data via insecure networks for the entity’s activities.[cite: 4] If the entity has remote workers, training should include guidance to ensure that all users securely configure their home network infrastructure.[cite: 4]
  * Train personnel in understanding malicious and unauthorised software, on the importance of malicious software detection and on the risks and consequences of using unauthorised software.[cite: 4]
* Offer employees contact points and resources for additional advice.[cite: 4]
* To implement the awareness raising programme, consult available sources, such as those from national or international cybersecurity organisations, ENISA’s AR-in-a-Box (78) and the Cybersecurity Skills Academy (79).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Awareness raising programme, that is, a comprehensive outline of the programme, detailing its objectives, content, frequency, syllabus and schedule.[cite: 4]
* Copies of the awareness-raising materials distributed to employees, including handouts, emails, presentations and online modules.[cite: 4]
* Logs, sign-in sheet, certificates of completion or acknowledgements given to employees upon completing the programme, showing which employees have taken part in the awareness-raising programme.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The awareness raising programme shall, where appropriate, be tested in terms of effectiveness.[cite: 4] The awareness raising programme shall be updated and offered at planned intervals taking into account changes in cyber hygiene practices, and the current threat landscape and risks posed to the relevant entities.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Offer cybersecurity awareness raising programmes periodically.[cite: 4]
* Test the effectiveness of the awareness raising programme for example by using quizzes or real scenarios.[cite: 4]
* Consider common KPIs (Annex to the regulation, point 7.2) to measure the effectiveness of the awareness-raising programme.[cite: 4]
* Review and update the awareness-raising programme at least annually.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Logs, sign-in sheets, certificates of completion or acknowledgements given to employees upon completing the programme showing which employees have taken part in the awareness-raising programme.[cite: 4]
* Results from any quizzes or assessments conducted to measure the employees’ understanding of the topics covered.[cite: 4]
* Employee feedback forms on the awareness raising programme, which can provide insight into the effectiveness of the programme and areas for improvement.[cite: 4]
* Reviewed and updated records showing that the programme is reviewed regularly and updated as necessary.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall identify employees, whose roles require security relevant skill sets and expertise and ensure that they receive regular training on network and information system security.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Assess which roles within the entity require security-relevant skills and expertise.[cite: 4]
* Offer training that focuses on the specific security skills required by the identified roles.[cite: 4]
* Consider globally recognized qualifications and certifications, and the ECSF (80).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* A comprehensive outline of the training programme, detailing the objectives for different roles and how to reach them, content and frequency of the training.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall establish, implement and apply a training program in line with the network and information security policy, topic-specific policies and other relevant procedures on network and information security which lays down the training needs for certain roles and positions based on criteria.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Provide role-specific network and information security training (81).[cite: 4]
* Consider various training methods, such as online courses, workshops, hands-on labs and simulations.[cite: 4]
* Consider various types of training, such as courses, certifications or attending security conferences or webinars, and the maintenance of certifications.[cite: 4]
* Examples of training may include secure system administration courses for IT professionals, Open Worldwide Application Security Project® awareness and prevention training for web application developers and advanced social engineering awareness training for high-profile roles.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* A comprehensive outline of the training programme, detailing the objectives for different roles and how to reach them, content and frequency of the training.[cite: 4]
* Assessment of effect and feedback from trainings.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The training referred to in point 8.2.1. shall be relevant to the job function of the employee and its effectiveness shall be assessed.[cite: 4] Training shall take into consideration security measures in place and cover the following:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: instructions regarding the secure configuration and operation of the network and information systems, including mobile devices;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: briefing on known cyber threats;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: training of the behaviour when security-relevant events occur.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Topics to include in the programme may include the following (indicative, non-exhaustive list).[cite: 4]
  * Train personnel in authentication best practices, such as MFA, password creation and credential management.[cite: 4]
  * Train personnel in how to identify and properly store, transfer, archive and destroy sensitive data.[cite: 4]
  * Train personnel to recognise a potential incident, such as unusual email attachments, unexpected system behaviour and suspicious network traffic.[cite: 4]
  * Train personnel in how to report events promptly and accurately, including the use of designated communication channels.[cite: 4]
  * Train personnel to understand how to verify and report out-of-date software or any failures in automated processes and tools.[cite: 4] Part of this training should include notifying IT personnel of any failures in automated processes and tools.[cite: 4]
  * Train relevant personnel in crisis management and business continuity procedures.[cite: 4] Incorporate simulated events (82) into crisis management training to facilitate an effective response by personnel in crisis situations.[cite: 4]
  * Train relevant personnel (e.g. system administrators and software developers) in the secure configuration and operation of the network and information systems.[cite: 4] Provide regular updates on the latest cyber threats.[cite: 4]
* Test the security knowledge of employees to make sure that it is sufficient and up to date.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Comprehensive outline of the training programme, detailing the objectives of different roles and how to reach them, and the content and frequency of the training.[cite: 4]
* Results from any quizzes or assessments conducted to measure the employees’ understanding of the topics covered.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall apply training to staff members who transfer to new positions or roles which require security relevant skill sets and expertise.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Examine whether the new position or role of an employee requires role-specific network and information security training.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Logs, sign-in sheets, certificates of completion or acknowledgements given to employees upon completing the training, showing that employees who transferred to new positions or roles attended training sessions relevant to the new position or role.[cite: 4]
* Evidence of maintenance of certifications obtained.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The program shall be updated and run periodically taking into account applicable policies and rules, assigned roles, responsibilities, as well as known cyber threats and technological developments.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Provide cybersecurity training periodically.[cite: 4]
* Review and update the training programme at least annually.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Logs, sign-in sheets, certificates of completion or acknowledgements given to employees upon completing the training, showing which employees attended the training sessions.[cite: 4]
* Information materials distributed to employees, including handouts, presentations and online modules.[cite: 4]
* Updates showing that the training programme is reviewed and updated regularly to keep up with the latest cybersecurity threats and best practices.[cite: 4]
* Employee feedback forms on the training sessions, which can provide insight into the effectiveness of the training and areas for improvement.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of Article 21(2), point (h) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the relevant entities shall establish, implement and apply a policy and procedures related to cryptography, with a view to ensuring adequate and effective use of cryptography to protect the confidentiality, authenticity and integrity of data in line with the relevant entities’ asset classification and the results of the risk assessment carried out pursuant to point 2.1.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Ensure that the comprehensive policy and procedures related to cryptography are in line with relevant regulations and state-of-the-art standards (83).[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Documented policy on cryptography and procedures related to cryptography.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The policy and procedures referred to in point 9.1 shall establish:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: in accordance with the relevant entities’ classification of assets, the type, strength and quality of the cryptographic measures required to protect the relevant entities’ assets, including data at rest and data in transit;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: based on point (a), the protocols or families of protocols to be adopted, as well as cryptographic algorithms, cipher strength, cryptographic solutions and usage practices to be approved and required for use in the relevant entities, following, where appropriate, a cryptographic agility approach;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the relevant entities’ approach to key management, including, where appropriate, methods for the following:[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the generating different keys for cryptographic systems and applications;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the issuing and obtaining public key certificates;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the distributing keys to intended entities, including how to activate keys when received;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the storing keys, including how authorised users obtain access to keys;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the changing or updating keys, including rules on when and how to change keys;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the dealing with compromised keys;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the revoking keys including how to withdraw or deactivate keys;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the recovering lost or corrupted keys;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the backing up or archiving keys;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the destroying keys;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the logging and auditing of key management-related activities;[cite: 4]

parts.name: item
parts.prose: the setting activation and deactivation dates for keys ensuring that the keys can only be used for the specified period of time according to the organization's rules on key management.[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The relevant entities shall review and, where appropriate, update their policy and procedures at planned intervals, taking into account the state of the art in cryptography.[cite: 4]

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Ensure the cryptography policy aligns with relevant industry standards and with advancements in the field.[cite: 4]
* Review the cryptography policy and procedures at least annually.[cite: 4]
* Maintain a procedure that specifies how reviews of the cryptography policy and procedures are conducted, including responsible personnel and review intervals.[cite: 4]
* Ensure that changes to the cryptographic measures are tested before being applied.[cite: 4]
* Ensure that changes to the cryptographic measures are communicated to employees.[cite: 4]

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* Logs of changes made to the cryptography policy and procedures[cite: 4]
* Test plans and results that demonstrate the implementation and effectiveness of updated cryptographic measures.[cite: 4]
* Records of notifications or reminders sent to relevant personnel about upcoming reviews of the cryptography policy and procedures.[cite: 4]
* Communication records informing personnel about updates to the cryptography policy following advancements in the field or significant changes.[cite: 4]
* Evidence that the entity remains up to date with the latest developments in cryptography (e.g. member of cryptographic bodies or consortia (e.g. Internet Engineering Task Force and cryptographic research groups) and subscriptions to cryptographic journals/feeds, mailing lists or news feeds).[cite: 4]

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: For the purpose of Article 21(2), point (i) of Directive (EU) 2022/2555, the relevant entities shall ensure that their employees and direct suppliers and service providers, wherever applicable, understand and commit to their security responsibilities, as appropriate for the offered services and the job and in line with the relevant entities’ policy on the security of network and information systems.

parts.name: guidance
parts.prose:
GUIDANCE

* Define clear security roles and responsibilities for employees, aligned with the entity’s security policies and each employee’s functional role. Define relevant security responsibilities for direct suppliers and service providers, within the scope of contractual obligations, ensuring they are appropriate to the nature of the services provided and aligned with the entity’s overall security requirements.
* Establish onboarding and continuous education programmes that include both security awareness and role-specific cybersecurity training tailored to different risk exposures.
* Implement periodic assessments to evaluate understanding of security responsibilities, supported by mandatory refresher training as needed.
* Ensure that security responsibilities are formally documented and integrated into job descriptions, contractual agreements and performance review processes. Incorporate relevant security responsibilities into contractual agreements or service-level agreements (SLA), for direct suppliers and service providers with clear language regarding expectations and compliance requirements.
* Promote a culture of accountability by requiring formal acknowledgement of security obligations and by linking compliance to incentives and disciplinary measures, where appropriate.
* Develop and maintain a centralized repository of training records, acknowledgements, certifications and contractual clauses to demonstrate compliance and facilitate audits.
* Require suppliers and service providers to designate responsible contacts for cybersecurity and encourage or mandate participation in relevant security briefings or training programmes provided by the entity.

parts.name: evidence
parts.prose:
EXAMPLES OF EVIDENCE

* List of employees whose roles require specific security skills and their assignment to roles.
* Documented evidence of regular training sessions on security of network and information systems for employees, direct suppliers and service providers, wherever applicable. This includes attendance records, training materials and feedback forms.
* Signed acknowledgements from employees, direct suppliers and service providers, wherever applicable, confirming they have read, understood and agreed to comply with the policy.
* Reports from internal or external audits assessing the understanding and implementation of security responsibilities among employees, direct suppliers and service providers, wherever applicable.
* Inclusion of security responsibilities, where relevant, in employee performance reviews and evaluations.
* Contracts with direct suppliers and service providers that include clauses on security responsibilities and compliance with the entity’s policies or written justifications by the direct supplier or service provider in cases where these clauses do not exist in the contract.
* Certifications or attestations of cybersecurity skills from nationally recognized or accredited bodies confirming that a person fulfils specific requirements regarding cybersecurity knowledge and skills.

parts.name: statement
parts.prose: The requirement referred to in point 10.1.1. shall include the following:

parts.name: item
parts.prose: mechanisms to ensure that all employees, direct suppliers and service providers, wherever applicable, understand and follow the standard cyber hygiene practices that the entities apply pursuant to point 8.1.;

parts.name: item
parts.prose: mechanisms to ensure that all users with administrative or privileged access are aware of and act in accordance with their roles, responsibilities and authorities;
